units.la: CLavium regni coelorum appellatio, seu Ministerialis potestas gubernandi Ecclesiam, desumpta est ex sermone Christi ad Petrum clavium ac disciplinae sub Novo Foedere auctoris, & Ecclesiae Domini, Apoc. 3. v. 7. qui illum in Ecclesia vigorem ac disciplinae ordinem instituit, Matth. 16. v. 19. Καὶ δώσω σοι τὰς κλεῖς τῆς βασιλείας τῶν οὐρανῶν. Et tibi dabo claves regni coelorum: per quas non intelligimus legum dispensationem, poenarum relaxationem, controversiarum fidei praetoriam decisionem; sed potestatem ligandi & solvendi, ut Exegeticè in hoc versu continetur. Καὶ ὃ ἐὰν δήσῃς ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, ἔσται δεδεμένον ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς, & quicquid ligaveris in terra, erit ligatum in coelis, & Matt. 18. v. 18. Joh. 20. v. 23. Ita ut methaphorica illa locutione significetur, peccatores impoenitentes, quorum peccata retinentur (i. e. non remittuntur propter impoenitentiam) ligatos esse, h.e. obligatos ad poenam, non enim statim conjicit in perpetuam ruinam, ac damnationem qui ligantur, sed vitam morésque damnat, quò praemoniti suae etiam ipsorum perpetuae damnationis, nisi resipuerint certi sint, quâ plectit hominem: sic tamen ut futurae damnationis praemoneat, & in salutem revocet. Peccatores vero poenitentes, quorum peccata remittuntur, solvit à vinculis, quibus constricti tenebantur; quaecunque enim Ecclesia pronunciat esse justa in his terris, seu in hoc mundo, Exod. 17. v. 14. Deut. 7. v. 6. 24. Eccl. 1. v. 13. & 2. v. 4. & 3. v. 1. Lament. 3. v. 66. Luc. 17. v. 24. Act. 2. v. 5. Col. 1. 23. ea Deus justa pronunciat in coelo, & quaecunque, causâ cognitâ, declarat esse injusta, ea Deus declarat esse injusta. In Scriptura sacra enim ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν, pro Ecclesia sumitur, Matt. 13. v. 24. 31. 33. 44. 45. 47. & cap. 20. v. 1. Act. 22. v. 2. & 25. 1. in quam interdictus est aditus ligato, soluto vero in eam aditus liber, & ex ea in coelum coelorum, Paradisum non manufactum, ubi satietas gaudiorum, Psal. 16. v. 11. Gaudium Domini, Matth. 25. v. 21. Gloria nostra, 1. Cor. 2. 7. 2. Thess. 1. v. 9. refrigerium, Act. 3. 19. Pax, Luc. 1. v. 79. felicitas omnium maxima, Psal. 31. v. 20. & 46. v. 5. 8. 1. Cor. 2. 9. Sic Graeci interpretantur. Ἐντεῦθεν ὁ Πέτρος τὸν Χριστὸν, ἡν Θεοῦ τὸ ζῶντος ὀνόματος, καὶ τὰς κλεῖς τῆς τῶν οὐρανῶν πιστεύει βασιλείας, ἵνα ἀνοίγῃ μὲν τοῖς πιστοῖς, ἀποκλείῃ δὲ τοῖς ἀπίστοις τῶν θείων ἀνακτόρων τὴν εἴσοδον. Hinc Petrum Christum Filium Dei nominavit, & ad hoc Claves regni Coelorum Petro credita, ut fidelibus aperiat fores sacrarum adium, infideles vero ab ingressu earum arceat, sic Augustinus in Johannem, Theophylactus in Matthaeum, Anselmus in eundem: sic & Judaei, siquidem verba ligare & solvere usitatissima fuere in Judaica Ecclesia, pro inde eo tempore, quo Christus in terris agebat, notissimae significationis, apud quos ligare significabat, interdicere אסר. Solvere vero, permittere, concedere, התיר. Dan. 6. 7. 17. Hinc dixerunt Davidem & Ezechielem nihil ligasse nisi quod esset ligatum in lege.
units.tr: The name "keys of the kingdom of heaven," or the ministerial power of governing the Church, is taken from Christ's words to Peter, the author under the New Covenant of the keys and of discipline, and of the Church of the Lord (Apoc. 3. v. 7), who established in the Church the vigour and order of discipline (Matth. 16. v. 19): "And I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven" [Καὶ δώσω σοι τὰς κλεῖς τῆς βασιλείας τῶν οὐρανῶν]. By these keys we do not understand the dispensing of laws, the remission of penalties, or the authoritative decision of controversies of faith, but the power of binding and loosing, as is set out explanatorily in this verse: "and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven" [καὶ ὃ ἐὰν δήσῃς ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, ἔσται δεδεμένον ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς], and in Matth. 18. v. 18 and Joh. 20. v. 23. So by that metaphorical expression it is signified that impenitent sinners, whose sins are retained (that is, not forgiven on account of their impenitence), are bound, that is, obligated to punishment. For those who are bound are not at once cast into everlasting ruin and damnation; rather, the Church condemns their life and morals, so that, forewarned of their own perpetual damnation unless they repent, they may be certain of the punishment that strikes the man. Yet it does so in such a way that it warns of future damnation and calls them back to salvation. But penitent sinners, whose sins are remitted, it looses from the chains by which they were held fast. For whatever the Church pronounces just in these lands, or in this world (Exod. 17. v. 14; Deut. 7. v. 6; 24; Eccl. 1. v. 13; 2. v. 4; 3. v. 1; Lament. 3. v. 66; Luc. 17. v. 24; Act. 2. v. 5; Col. 1. 23), God pronounces just in heaven; and whatever the Church, once the cause has been known, declares to be unjust, God declares to be unjust. In Holy Scripture the "kingdom of heaven" is indeed taken for the Church (Matth. 13. v. 24, 31, 33, 44, 45, 47; and chap. 20. v. 1; Act. 22. v. 2; and 25. 1), into which entry is forbidden to the bound but open to the loosed; and from it entry is open into the "heaven of heavens," a Paradise not made by hands, where there is "fullness of joys" (Psal. 16. v. 11), "the joy of the Lord" (Matth. 25. v. 21), "our glory" (1 Cor. 2. 7; 2 Thess. 1. v. 9), "refreshment" (Act. 3. 19), "peace" (Luc. 1. v. 79), "the greatest happiness of all" (Psal. 31. v. 20; and 46. v. 5, 8; 1 Cor. 2. 9). So the Greeks interpret it: "Hence Peter, acknowledging Christ to be the Son of the living God, believes that he holds the keys of the kingdom of heaven, so that he may open the doors to the faithful and shut out the unbelieving from entering the divine sanctuary" [Ἐντεῦθεν ὁ Πέτρος τὸν Χριστὸν, ἡν Θεοῦ τὸ ζῶντος ὀνόματος, καὶ τὰς κλεῖς τῆς τῶν οὐρανῶν πιστεύει βασιλείας, ἵνα ἀνοίγῃ μὲν τοῖς πιστοῖς, ἀποκλείῃ δὲ τοῖς ἀπίστοις τῶν θείων ἀνακτόρων τὴν εἴσοδον]. Hence he named Peter as the one who called Christ the Son of God; and for this purpose the keys of the kingdom of heaven were entrusted to Peter, so that he might open the doors of the holy house to the faithful and keep the unbelieving from entering. So Augustine on John, Theophylact on Matthew, and Anselm on the same passage. So too the Jews, since to bind and to loose were the most common expressions in the Jewish Church, and at the time when Christ was living on earth they had a well-known meaning: among them "to bind" meant to forbid [אסר], and "to loose," to permit or grant [התיר] (Dan. 6. 7, 17). Hence they said that David and Ezekiel bound nothing except what was already bound in the law.

units.tr: This promise of the keys of the kingdom of heaven was not made to Peter alone, although the Lord addressed the keys to him alone (Matth. 16. v. 19). It was made to the whole college of the apostles after him, with a singular and infallible authority, since they were endowed with equal dignity and authority by Christ, who chose and sent them directly and furnished them with the power of preaching (Matth. 4. v. 19; Marc. 3. v. 13, 14; Luc. 6. v. 13, 14, 15; Joh. 4. v. 38; Act. 1. v. 2; and 26. v. 24; and 26. v. 16, 17; Rom. 1. v. 5; Gal. 1. vers. 1; compare Matth. 18. v. 1, 2, 3, 4; Marc. 9. v. 33, 34; Luc. 9. v. 48; Marc. 6. v. 7; Joh. 20. v. 21, 22, 23; Act. 1. v. 8; 26; and 2. v. 4; and 6. v. 2; and 8. v. 14; and 13. vers. 32; 2 Cor. 11. v. 5; and 12. v. 11; Gal. 1. v. 17, 18, 19; and 2. v. 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13; Apoc. 21. 14), and after their death to the ordinary ministers of the Church. It is clear from the question Christ asked, not only of Peter but of his fellows also (v. 15): "But who do you say that I am?" [ὑμεῖς δὲ τίνα με λέγετε εἶναι;]. Peter answered (v. 16) not in his own name only but in the name of the apostles: "You are Christ, the Son of the living God" [Σὺ εἶ ὁ Χριστὸς, ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ ζῶντος], which he drew from the prophets (Psal. 45. v. 8; Esa. 6. v. 1), not acquired by flesh and blood (Matth. 16. v. 17); this confession was shared by the others as well (Matth. 14. v. 33; Joh. 1. v. 50). So Christ now says to him (Joh. 21. 15, 16): "Feed my sheep," that is, rule, govern the Church, preach the Word, administer the sacraments, teach, exhort, rebuke (Cant. 1. v. 8; Esa. 61. v. 5; Ezech. 34 v. 2; Zach. 11. v. 4, 7; Joh. 21. v. 15, 16; Act. 20. v. 28; 2 Tim. 3. 15, 16; 1 Pet. 5. v. 2). This is common to all ministers of the Church (Esa. 6 5. v. 2; Jer. 3 5. v. 1, 5; Hos. 5. v. 1; Joel 2. v. 12; Matth. 3. vers. 1; Luc. 3. v. 18; Act. 2. v. 40; and 11. v. 23; and 14. v. 22; and 15. v. 31, 32; and 20. v. 21, 28, 31; Rom. 12. v. 1; and 15. v. 30; 1 Cor. 1. 10; 2 Cor. 6. 1; Phil. 3. 3. v. 2; 1 Thess. 2. v. 11; and 3. v. 2; and 4. v. 10; 2 Thess. 3. v. 12; 1 Tim. 2. v. 1; and 5. v. 1; and 6. v. 2; 2 Tim. 4. v. 2). Therefore they do not claim for Peter any authority of supreme judgment, against the Papists; for the apostles knew that this lordship was forbidden (Matth. 20. v. 25, 26; and 23. v. 12; Marc. 10. v. 43; Luc. 22. v. 25, 26; Phil. 2. v. 5, 6, 7; 1 Pet. 5. 3). Pope Pelagius II, Bishop of Rome, also acknowledged this, for he speaks thus in the Decretals, distinct. 40: "Let none of the patriarchs use so profane a title"; and "if one of the patriarchs is called universal, the name of patriarch is taken away from the rest"; and "whoever desires the primacy on earth will find confusion in heaven." Nor shall he be counted among the servants of Christ who "has treated of the primacy." So also Gregory I speaks in book 6, letter 24: "I confidently say that whoever calls himself, or desires to be called, universal priest, in his arrogance runs before Antichrist."

units.la: De hac clavium potestate, non soli Petro; sed toti Apostolorum collegio facta, ita etiam Patres loquuntur. Augustinus in Matthæum, & in Psalmum 87. 88. Respondet (inquit) Petrus pro omnibus, pro unitate unus. Ambrosius in Ps. 38. Quod (inquit) Petro dicitur, Apostolis dicitur. Patian. Epist. 1. ad Sympro: Hieronymus lib. 1. adversus Jovin. Origines in Matthæum, Cyprianus de unitate Ecclesiæ. Basilius de Constitut. Moral. Gaudentius, Theophylactus in Matt. 16. Etsi Petro promittitur peculiariter, tamen nihil promittit peculiare: & id quod promittebatur non est jus speciale, in cujus usurpatione socium non admitteret, hoc est promissionem seu actum promittendi fuisse Petro peculiarem; sed non rem ipsam quæ promittebatur tur. 1. Q. eo jure quod tum Petro promittebatur non solus Petrus usus est; sed tota Ecclesia & omnes Episcopi 2. Quia id omnibus Apostolis postea à Christo concessum, tum iisdem verbis Matt. 18. v. 18 tum æquipollentibus Joh. 20. 23. 3. Quia tum Petrus figuram gestavit totius militantis Ecclesiæ: exist imandum est ergò, quæ Petro dicta sunt, Ecclesiæ dicta esse: ut in Petro Ecclesia, in Petro Episcopi claves regni cœlorum acceperint. 4. Quia dum Petrus videret totum Collegium à Domino interrogatum, solus pro omnibus respondit. Vide simile Matt. 4. v. 19. Simoni & Andreæ dixit Dominus, sequimini, faciam vos piscatores hominum: hic actus promittendi non alios respexit, quàm illos duos, res ipsa tamen fuit communis cum reliquis.
units.tr: That this power of the keys was given not to Peter alone but to the whole college of the Apostles, the Fathers also teach. Augustine, on Matthew and on Psalm 87 (88): Peter answers (he says) for all, one for the unity. Ambrose, on Psalm 38: What is said to Peter is said to the Apostles. Paulinus, Epistle 1 to Symmachus; Jerome, book 1 against Jovinian; Origen on Matthew; Cyprian, On the Unity of the Church; Basil, On the Moral Constitutions; Gaudentius; Theophylact on Matthew 16. Although the promise is made to Peter in a peculiar way, it promises nothing peculiar: and what was promised is not a special right, in the exercise of which he would admit no partner. That is, the promise or the act of promising was peculiar to Peter, but not the thing itself that was promised. This is shown: (1) because the right that was then promised to Peter was not used by Peter alone, but by the whole Church and all bishops; (2) because it was afterwards granted by Christ to all the Apostles, in the same words in Matt. 18:18 and in equivalent words in John 20:23; (3) because Peter then bore the figure of the whole militant Church. It must therefore be concluded that what was said to Peter was said to the Church, so that in Peter the Church, and in Peter the bishops, received the keys of the kingdom of heaven; (4) because, while Peter saw the whole college questioned by the Lord, he alone answered for all. Compare Matt. 4:19, where the Lord said to Simon and Andrew, Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men. That act of promising looked only to those two, but the thing itself was common to the rest.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Potestas hæc clavium licèt communis sit cum Ministris Ecclesiæ N. T. tamen inclinato sensu & minori cum auctoritate, hi acceperunt quàm isti, à dispensatore clavium, siquidem vocatio illorum generalis fuit, nullis certis Civitatum, distr ictuum, aut regionum limitibus coarctata; sed extendens se ad universum orbem; seu ad omnes gentes, ut patet. I. Ex locis clarissimis S. sacræ, Matt. 28. 19. Profecti docete omnes gentes, baptizantes in nomine Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. Mar. 16. v. 15. [Syriac text, illegible, ~20 letters] Luc. 24. 47. 48. Joh. 17. 18. & 20. 21. Act. 1. 8. & 20. 15. Rom. 1. 5. & 10. 18. Col. 1. 6. 23. 1. Tim. 3. 16. Deus conspicuus factus est in carne, prædicatus gentibus, fides illi habita est in mundo. De quo opere loquens Chrysostomus homilia 4. in Epist. 1. ad Cor. sic ait: Apostoli brevi tempore omnem terram, tanquam alati percurrerunt, hinc dicuntur sal terræ & lux mundi Matt. 5. v. 13. 14. II. Ex innummerarum Ecclesiarum ad Christum adductarum serie, quarum ex Scriptura catalogus texitur. Samaria enim fuit, Actor. 8. 14. In vicus Samaria, v. 25. Damasci, Act. 9. 19. 20. Lydda, v. 32. In Joppe, v. 36. 38. In Cæsarea, Act. 10. 1. 2. 3. In Antiochia, Act. 11. 20. 26. In Salamine, Act. 13. 5. In Papho, Act. 13. 6. In Antiochia Pisidiæ, Act. 13. v. 14. In Iconio, Act. 14. 1. In Syria & Cilicia, Act. 15. 23. In Lystra & Derbe, Act. 14. 6. 20. 21. In Pergâ, 14. v. 25. Philippis, Act. 16. 12. & 20. v. 6. In Lydia, Act. 16. 40. In Thessalonica, Act. 17. 1. 2. In Epheso, Act. 18. v. 19. & 19. v. 1. In Galatia & Phrygia, Act. 18. 23. In Troja de Act. 20. 5. 6. 7. In Asso, v. 13. In Tyro, Act. 21. 3. 4. In Ptolomaide, v. 7. &c. Horum verò definita certum in locum inclusa Act. 20. 28. Attendite igitur animum ad vos ipsos & totum gregem, in quo vos Spiritus ille sanctus constituit Episcopos, ad pascendam Ecclesiam, quam suo illo proprio sanguine acquisivit. 1. Pet. 5. versz. Quorum etiam Ministrorum Dei est, ut portent nomen Christi in conspectu hominum, Act.9.15. (pro Christo enim legatione funguntur Rom.1.5. 2.Cor.5.v.20.) evangelizent impervestigabiles Dei opes, Eph.3.7.8. testificentur gratiam Dei, Act.20.24. 1.Pet.5.2. aperiant oculos hominum, Act.26.vers.18. convertant eos à tenebris ad lucem, à potestate Satanæ ad Deum, v.18. adducant eos ad obedientiam fidei, Rom.1.v.5. pascant Ecclesiam. Jer.23.v.4. Joh.21.15.16. Acto.20.vers.28. 1.Pet.5.2. Ut corpus Christi mysticum constituatur, Eph.4.v.12. Hinc Hieronymus: Si quis igitur non ædificat Ecclesiam, nec plebem sibi subjectam instruit, ut de subjecto populo Christi Ecclesia constituatur, iste nec Apostolus, nec Propheta, nec Evangelista, nec Pastor, nec Magister est apellandus, non enim ad otium, ad honores, aut ad opes mundanas parandas, sed ad labores & sudores vocantur Ministri.
units.tr: Although this power of the keys is common to the ministers of the church of the New Testament, yet those received it from the Steward of the keys with a lower sense and less authority than these do. For their calling was general, not confined to any certain limits of cities, districts or regions, but extending to the whole world, that is, to all nations, as is evident. I. From the clearest passages of Holy Scripture: Matt. 28:19, Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Mark 16:15; [Syriac text, illegible in the scan]; Luke 24:47-48; John 17:18 and 20:21; Acts 1:8 and 20:15; Rom. 1:5 and 10:18; Col. 1:6, 23; 1 Tim. 3:16, God was manifested in the flesh, preached among the Gentiles, believed on in the world. Speaking of this work, Chrysostom, Homily 4 on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, says thus: The Apostles ran through the whole earth in a short time, as if they had wings; hence they are called the salt of the earth and the light of the world, Matt. 5:13-14. II. From the series of countless churches brought to Christ, whose catalogue is woven from Scripture. Samaria was one, Acts 8:14; in the villages of Samaria, v. 25; Damascus, Acts 9:19-20; Lydda, v. 32; in Joppa, vv. 36, 38; in Caesarea, Acts 10:1-3; in Antioch, Acts 11:20, 26; in Salamis, Acts 13:5; in Paphos, Acts 13:6; in Antioch of Pisidia, Acts 13:14; in Iconium, Acts 14:1; in Syria and Cilicia, Acts 15:23; in Lystra and Derbe, Acts 14:6, 20-21; in Perga, 14:25; at Philippi, Acts 16:12 and 20:6; in Lydia, Acts 16:40; in Thessalonica, Acts 17:1-2; in Ephesus, Acts 18:19 and 19:1; in Galatia and Phrygia, Acts 18:23; at Troas, Acts 20:5-7; at Assos, v. 13; at Tyre, Acts 21:3-4; at Ptolemais, v. 7, etc. But these were enclosed within definite places. Acts 20:28, Take heed therefore to yourselves and to all the flock, over which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to feed the Church of God, which he purchased with his own blood; 1 Pet. 5. To these ministers of God it also belongs to bear the name of Christ before men, Acts 9:15 (for they act as ambassadors for Christ, Rom. 1:5; 2 Cor. 5:20), to preach the unsearchable riches of God, Eph. 3:7-8, to testify the grace of God, Acts 20:24; 1 Pet. 5:2, to open the eyes of men, Acts 26:18, to turn them from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, v. 18, to bring them to the obedience of faith, Rom. 1:5, to feed the Church, Jer. 23:4; John 21:15-16; Acts 20:28; 1 Pet. 5:2, so that the mystical body of Christ may be built up, Eph. 4:12. Hence Jerome: If anyone, then, does not build the Church, nor instruct the people committed to him, so that from the subject people a church of Christ may be formed, he is not to be called an Apostle, nor a Prophet, nor an Evangelist, nor a Pastor, nor a Teacher; for ministers are called not to leisure, honours, or the acquiring of worldly wealth, but to labours and sweat.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Potestatis clavium Regni cœlorum appellatio in N.T. est metaphorica, non propria, similitudine quadam ab œconomis, administratoribus domus, translata: Sicut enim illi traditione clavium confirmari solent in suo munere & officio, ut Eliachim tanquam primarius Regis Ezechiæ officiarius, recipiendo claves domus Davidis, Esa.22.22. est confirmatus ad magnum & liberum munus in domo Davidis exercendum; fuit enim acceptio clavium olim signum magnæ dignitatis: Sic Deus in Ecclesia, quæ ipsius domus est, allusive ad Tabernaculum & Templum sierosolymitanum, Num.12.7. 1.Chro.17.14.Psal.23.6. & 27.v.4. & 36.v.9. & 52.v.10.& 65.v.5.& 92.v.14.& 93.v.5. & 118.v.26. & 122.v.9.Prov.9.v.1. Servos suos, Rom.1.v.1. Phil.1.v.1. Tit.1.v.1. veluti œconomos, 1.Cor.4.v.1. potestate ligandi & solvendi, tanquam clavibus quibusdam auctoravit, non tamen supremâ & absoluta; Christus enim eam tanquam absolutus Dominus & Princeps Ecclesiæ habet, Apoc.3.v.7. Sed Ministeriali, sunt enim servi Dei, & præcones Evangelii, Luc.1.76.77.& ut v.47. Act.13.38.26.18.24. Ambrosius lib.1.de Spiritu S. c.19. loquitur: Peccata nemo condonat, nisi unus Deus. Homines autem in remissione peccatorum, ministerium exhibent, non jus alicujus potestatis exercent, annunciando scil: doctrinam Evangelii de remissione peccatorum, Matt.16.19. & 18.v.18. Joh.20.23. Posceret quidem hic analogia methaphoræ, ut Matthæus uteretur aperiendi & claudendi vocabulis, sicut fecit Esa.22.v.22. Et posteum Johannes Apocalypticus, Apoc. 3. 7. Maluit tamen Spir. S. ligandi & solvendi verba usurpare: ut intelligamus, quam misera sit conditio eorum, qui ligantur in peccatis suis; contrà verò, quam beati sunt illi, qui solvuntur à vinculis suorum peccatorum, quoniam haeredes seu possessio [Hebrew] Deo grata, & dulcis sunt; Sicut [Hebrew] unicuique dulcis & jucunda solet esse haereditas, quam possidet, Exod. 15. v. 17. Deut. 4. v. 20. & 32. v. 9. 1. Sam. 10. v. 1. 2. Sam. 21. 3. 1. Reg. 8. 51. 53. 2. Reg. 21. 14. Psal. 28. 9. & 33. v. 12. & 47. v. 5. & 74. v. 2. Esa. 19. v. 25. Jerem. 10. 16. Joel. 2. 17. Mich. 7. 14. 18. Zach. 2. 12. 1. Pet. 5. 3.
units.tr: The expression "power of the keys of the kingdom of heaven" is metaphorical, not literal, in the New Testament. It is transferred by a certain likeness from stewards, the administrators of a household. Just as such men are usually confirmed in their office and duty by the handing over of keys, so Eliakim, the chief officer of King Hezekiah, was confirmed by receiving the keys of David's house (Isa. 22:22) for the great and free office to be exercised in David's house. For the receiving of keys was once a sign of great dignity. So God, in the Church, which is his house, alluding to the tabernacle and temple of Jerusalem (Num. 12:7; 1 Chron. 17:14; Ps. 23:6; 27:4; 36:9; 52:10; 65:5; 92:14; 93:5; 118:26; 122:9; Prov. 9:1), has empowered his servants (Rom. 1:1; Phil. 1:1; Tit. 1:1), as stewards (1 Cor. 4:1), with the power of binding and loosing, as with certain keys. It is not, however, a supreme and absolute power, for Christ holds that as the absolute Lord and Prince of the Church (Rev. 3:7). Theirs is a ministerial power, for they are servants of God and heralds of the gospel (Luke 1:76-77 and v. 47; Acts 13:38; 26:18; 24). Ambrose, in On the Holy Spirit, book 1, chapter 19, says: No one forgives sins but the one God. Men, however, in the remission of sins, perform a ministry; they do not exercise the right of any power, namely, by announcing the doctrine of the gospel concerning the remission of sins (Matt. 16:19; 18:18; John 20:23). Admittedly, the analogy of the metaphor would have required Matthew to use the words "opening" and "shutting," as Isaiah did (22:22), and afterwards John in the Apocalypse (Rev. 3:7). Yet the Holy Spirit preferred to use the words "binding" and "loosing," so that we may understand how wretched is the condition of those who are bound in their sins, and, on the contrary, how blessed are those who are loosed from the chains of their sins, since the inheritance or possession [Hebrew] is pleasing and sweet to God, just as an inheritance that a person possesses is usually sweet and pleasant to him (Exod. 15:17; Deut. 4:20; 32:9; 1 Sam. 10:1; 2 Sam. 21:3; 1 Kings 8:51, 53; 2 Kings 21:14; Ps. 28:9; 33:12; 47:5; 74:2; Isa. 19:25; Jer. 10:16; Joel 2:17; Mic. 7:14, 18; Zech. 2:12; 1 Pet. 5:3).

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Catechesis claves regni coelorum bifariam describit. 1. Distributione partium. Sunt enim geminae, praedicatio Evangelii & [Hebrew] disciplina Ecclesiastica. Mediantibus enim his duobus coelum aperiunt & claudunt, ligant & solvunt, peccata retinent & remittunt Ministri Ecclesiarum N.T. annunciando resipiscentibus miseri cordiam Dei, & quòd remissa sunt illis peccata; Incredulis verò & impoenitentibus iram Dei, & quòd non sunt illis remissa peccata, atque ira pronunciant illos qui dem pertinere ad Ecclesiam. Hos verò excludi ex ea, & consequenter ex regno coelorum: has claves Pontificii in Ordinis & Jurisdictionis dispescunt, quarum illas Presbyteris, has tantùm Ministris & Episcopis concedunt, quod discrimen Presbyteri & Episcopi Scripturae sacrae est apocryphum. Ex nostris etiam, in clavem scientiae & regiminis fundamento loci Luc. 11. 52. Va vobis legis interpretibus, quoniam sustulistis Clavem cognitionis; ipsi non introivistis, & eos qui intrabant prohibuistis: ubi per clavem cognitionis (τὴν κλεῖδα τῆς γνώσεως) potestas & jus seu munus docendi & interpretandi Scripturas S. Pastoribus collatum, ut ea recte fungentes, deducant homines ad Dei vivi cognitionem, quae aperit mysterium regni coelorum, ut aditus pateat, sicut clave aperiuntur aedes ut aditus in eas sit liber, quas legis interpretes auferebant: de quibus Theophylactus. Januas legis (cujus cognitio erat manductio ad Christum) non aperiebant, ut per eas intrarent, & ipsi & populus ad Christum: Clavem Regiminis iterum. I. In clavem Ministerii, cui verbi praedicationem, Sacramentorum administrationem. II. In ordinis, cui conservationem doctrinae in integritate. III. In correptionis, cui disciplinam Ecclesiasticam tribuunt: quae divisio non parvo incommodo laborat. II. Expositione finis & usûs contrarii circa objecta contraria: Quod cœlum aperiant fidelibus: infidelibus verò claudant. Matt. 16. 19. Joh. 20. 23. Matt. 18. 18.
units.tr: The Catechism describes the keys of the kingdom of heaven in two ways. 1. By the division of parts. There are two: the preaching of the gospel and church discipline [Hebrew]. For through these two the ministers of the churches of the New Testament open and shut heaven, bind and loose, retain and remit sins. They announce to the repentant the mercy of God and that their sins are forgiven them; but to the unbelieving and impenitent they announce the wrath of God and that their sins are not forgiven, and they declare that such persons are not in the Church and, consequently, are excluded from the kingdom of heaven. The Papists divide these keys into the keys of order and of jurisdiction, granting the former to presbyters and the latter only to ministers and bishops. This distinction between presbyter and bishop is apocryphal in Holy Scripture. Among our own writers, the key of knowledge and of government is also found, on the basis of Luke 11:52: Woe to you lawyers, for you have taken away the key of knowledge; you yourselves did not enter, and you hindered those who were entering. Here, by the key of knowledge (τὴν κλεῖδα τῆς γνώσεως), is meant the power, right, or office of teaching and interpreting the Scriptures, given to the pastors, so that by fulfilling it rightly they may lead men to the knowledge of the living God, which opens the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, so that the way lies open, just as houses are opened with a key so that access to them is free. The lawyers were taking this away. On this Theophylact says: They did not open the doors of the law (whose knowledge was a leading to Christ), so that they and the people might enter through them to Christ. Again, the key of government: I. The key of the ministry, to which belong the preaching of the Word and the administration of the sacraments. II. The key of order, to which belongs the preservation of doctrine in its integrity. III. The key of correction, to which they assign church discipline. This division suffers from no small inconvenience. II. By the exposition of the contrary end and use in regard to contrary objects: that they open heaven to the faithful, but shut it against the unbelieving (Matt. 16:19; John 20:23; Matt. 18:18).

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Prima clavis œconomiæ Ecclesiasticæ, quæ prædicatione Evangelii constat, est jus Ecclesiæ, quo ordine certo, sacris literis consentaneo, observato, utitur in verbo Dei publicè prædicando, sacramentis administrandis & controversiis, de doctrina fidei, ex verbo Dei per Spiritus S. gratiam decidendis. Seu, est, qua voluntas seu mandatum, statutum, decretum, & beneplacitum Dei, Esd. 10. v. 11. Psal. 40. 9. Matt. 7. 21. & 12. v. 50. Mar. 3. 35. Joh. 4. 34 & 7. 17. & 9. v. 31. Act. 13. v. 22. Eph. 6. v. 6. Heb. 10. 36. & 13. v. 21. proponitur seu traditur, exponitur, perspicuè, dilucidè, aperte, omni obscuritate, & ambiguitate remotâ. Sic enim debemus statuta, præcepta Dei proponere, Exod. 19. verf. 7. Deut. 4. verf. 8. Jef. 24. v. 25. 2 Sam. 24. 1. Chr. 12. 21. v. 10. 1 Reg. 9. 6. 2. Chron. 7. 19. Dan. 9. v. 10. Benedictionem, maledictionem. Benedictionem si auscultaverit Jehova, Deut. 11. 27. Maledictionem, si non auscultaverit Præceptis Jehova, v. 28. Bonum ac Malum Deut. 30. 15. 19. vitam ac mortem הַחַיִּים והַמָּוֶת. viam vitæ & mortis את־דֶּרֶךְ החיים ואת־דֶּרֶךְ המות ad fidem & obedientiam gignendam, Rom. 1. verf. 5. invictam constantiam confessoribus, Act. 6. 51. verf. 63. ingenerandam. Penetrantior enim est quovis gladio ancipiti, ad ipsam enim animam pertingit Heb. 4. 12. 10. Ne ergò verbum Dei contemnamus. Psal. 119. v. 21. 118. 119. 155. Exemplo Judæorum. Act. 7. 39. 51. Ne illud vel ipsi corrumpamus, vel nostra negligentia corrumpi sinamus: Exemplo Diaboli Matt. 4. 6. Theræ, Jos. 24. v. 2. Israëlitarum in Ægypto, Ezech. 20. 7. 8. 9. Haereticorum, 2 Tim. 2. 18. 2. Pet. 3. 17. ne ullis libris literisve tantum temporis & studii, atque huic impendamus, Psal. 1. v. 2. Deut. 6. v. 7. 8. 9. ne supra illud sapiamus, 1 Cor. 4. v. 6. Rom. 12. v. 3. aut contra illud ratiocinia vanámque Philosophiam audiamus, Col. 2. v. 8. Vanam dicimus, ut distinguamus à sana & meliori Philosophia, toti orbi & omni syncero Theologo commendatissima. Qua singulari felicitate sæculum ornavit Nob. Renatus Cartesius qui raro & inaudito hactenus exemplo, exuto præjudiciis animo, in vacuum posuit vestigia Princeps, & non sensibus, sed menti, insitisque illi principiis, simplicissimis & generalissimis, superstruens solidiorem Philosophiam, continuo filo ita primis extrema coaptavit, ut integram Microcosmi & Macrocosmi naturam inde reseraverit. verit. Hanc non detestamur, sed Atheniensium illam Act. 17.32. & Corinthiorum nonnullorum, 1. Cor. 15.
units.tr: The first key of ecclesiastical economy, which consists in the preaching of the gospel, is the right of the Church, which it uses, observing a fixed order consonant with the sacred letters, in publicly preaching the Word of God, administering the sacraments, and deciding controversies concerning the doctrine of faith from the Word of God through the grace of the Holy Spirit. Or it is the means by which the will, command, statute, decree, and good pleasure of God (Ezra 10:11; Ps. 40:9; Matt. 7:21; 12:50; Mark 3:35; John 4:34; 7:17; 9:31; Acts 13:22; Eph. 6:6; Heb. 10:36; 13:21) is set forth or handed down, explained clearly, plainly, and openly, with all obscurity and ambiguity removed. For thus we ought to set forth the statutes and precepts of God (Exod. 19:7; Deut. 4:8; Josh. 24:25; 2 Sam. 24:1; 1 Chron. 12:21; 2 Chron. 7:19; 1 Kings 9:6; Dan. 9:10): the blessing and the curse. The blessing, if you hearken to the LORD (Deut. 11:27); the curse, if you do not hearken to the precepts of the LORD (v. 28); good and evil (Deut. 30:15, 19); life and death [Hebrew]; the way of life and the way of death [Hebrew], for the begetting of faith and obedience (Rom. 1:5); for engendering an unconquered constancy in confessors (Acts 6:15; 7:51, 63). For it is more piercing than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the soul (Heb. 4:12; 10). Therefore let us not despise the Word of God (Ps. 119:21, 118, 119, 155). Let us not follow the example of the Jews (Acts 7:39, 51), nor corrupt it ourselves, nor allow it to be corrupted by our negligence, following the example of the devil (Matt. 4:6), of Terah (Josh. 24:2), of the Israelites in Egypt (Ezek. 20:7-9), or of heretics (2 Tim. 2:18; 2 Pet. 3:17). Nor should we spend so much time and zeal on any books or writings apart from it (Ps. 1:2; Deut. 6:7-9). Let us not be wise beyond what is written (1 Cor. 4:6; Rom. 12:3), nor listen to reasonings and vain philosophy against it (Col. 2:8). We say "vain" in order to distinguish it from sound and better philosophy, most commended to the whole world and to every sincere theologian. With singular felicity the noble René Descartes has adorned our age. With a rare and hitherto unheard-of example, having laid aside his prejudices, he set his feet on ground that had not been trodden before, a prince of philosophy. Building not on the senses but on the mind and the simplest and most general principles innate in it, he erected a more solid philosophy. By a continuous thread he so joined the extremes to the first principles that he unlocked from them the whole nature of the microcosm and the macrocosm. We do not reject this; rather, we reject that of the Athenians (Acts 17:32) and of some of the Corinthians (1 Cor. 15:12).

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Hæc prima Clavis œconomiæ Ecclesiasticæ declaratur. I. A' Causa, quæ est institutio & ordinatio Divina, cui placuit prædicationem instituere. 1. Cor. 1.21. & Ministros Ecclesiæ ab ipso Matrum utero ad prædicandum Evangelium segregare, Rom. 1.v.1. Gal. 1.15.16. ut prædicationem eis committat. 1. Thess. 2.4. ab illo enim tota vis & efficacia pendet prædicationis, Act. 14.v.17. & 16.v.14. 1. Cor. 3.6.7. & 16.v.7. 2. Cor 2.12. Tribuitur autem Deo non modo communiter secundum essentiam, sed etiam secundum personas singulariter. Etenim Deus Pater in V.T. πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως Heb. 1.v.1. cum Patriarchis & Prophetis, tum populo Israëlitico in Monte Sinai, Exod. 20. Ejusque duci Moysi, Exod. 33.11. Num. 12.8. Deut. 34.10. & in N. Testamento cœlitus clara voce est locutus, Matt. 3.19.17. & 17.v.5. Joh. 12.28. Sic & Filius viva voce usus est: in Vet. Testamento jam hominis, Gen. 48.16. Jud. 6.11. & seqq. forma tectus, in Novo autem natura humana in personæ suæ unitatem assumpta vestitus: Spiritus sanctus denique idem utroque Testamento mediante peregit.
units.tr: This is the first key of the economy of the Church, and it is set out as follows. I. From the cause, which is divine institution and ordinance: it pleased God to institute preaching (1 Cor. 1:21), and to set apart the ministers of the Church from their mother's womb to preach the Gospel (Rom. 1:1; Gal. 1:15-16), so that he might entrust preaching to them (1 Thess. 2:4). For all the power and efficacy of preaching depends on him (Acts 14:17; 16:14; 1 Cor. 3:6-7; 16:7; 2 Cor. 2:12). This is ascribed to God not only in general according to his essence, but also to each person in particular. For God the Father in the Old Testament spoke in many parts and in many ways [πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως] (Heb. 1:1), both with the Patriarchs and Prophets and with the people of Israel on Mount Sinai (Exod. 20), and with its leader Moses (Exod. 33:11; Num. 12:8; Deut. 34:10). In the New Testament he spoke from heaven with a clear voice (Matt. 3:17; 17:5; John 12:28). So too the Son used the living voice: in the Old Testament clothed in the form of a man (Gen. 48:16; Judg. 6:11ff.), but in the New in human nature, assumed into the unity of his person. Finally, the Holy Spirit worked through both Testaments in the same way.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.tr: II. From the subjects who preach: such as Noah, who preached to men (1 Pet. 3:19), whence he is called a herald of the righteousness of God (2 Pet. 2:5); priests and prophets (Gen. 14:18; Exod. 31:10; Lev. 14:12; Num. 15:25; Deut. 24:8; Josh. 6:4; Judg. 18:4; 1 Sam. 2:35; 1 Chron. 6:41; Ps. 132:9; Isa. 61:6; Jer. 23:33; Lam. 1:19; Ezek. 45:4; Joel 1:9; Hag. 2:12); John the Baptist (Matt. 3:1; 11:11; 14:2; Mark 1:3-4; Luke 3:3-4, 18; John 1:23; Acts 10:37; 13:24); Christ made manifest in the flesh (Matt. 4:17; 23:9, 35; Mark 1:38; Luke 4:18; John 18:19; Rom. 16:25). Clement of Alexandria, in the first book of the Stromata, says that he preached for one year; Epiphanius, two; Origen, in the second book on John, three and a half; Eusebius, in Ecclesiastical History book 1 chapter 10, about four. Scaliger says four years and more, which opinion seems to us the most correct. The apostles (Matt. 10:2; Mark 6:30; Luke 6:13; 9:1, 10; 11:49; 17:5; 22:14; 24:10; Acts 4:33; 15:6; Rom. 1:1; 1 Cor. 1:1; 2 Cor. 8:23; Gal. 1:1; Eph. 4:11; Phil. 2:25; Col. 1:1; 1 Thess. 2:7; 1 Tim. 1:2, 11; 1 Pet. 1:1; Jude 17; Rev. 18:20), whom Christ called and sent to preach the Gospel, first indeed into Judea (Matt. 10:6), and at last into the whole world (Matt. 28:19); pastors (Jer. 3:10; 23:4; 25:34; Ezek. 34:23); evangelists (Isa. 41:27; Acts 8:4; 21:8; 2 Cor. 2:12; Eph. 4:11; 2 Tim. 4:5; Rev. 10:7; 14; 6).

units.la: III. Declaratur ab objecto; sunt enim circa quos exercetur, [illegible, ~6 letters] prædicatio, vel [illegible, ~6 letters] fideles, vel infideles, & Hypocritæ, Fidelibus sive universis, sive singulis, publicè annunciatur [illegible, ~6 letters] remissio peccatorum, & vita æterna, propter meritum Jesu fide apprehensum, in promissione Evangelii, Matth. 9. 2. & 25. v. 46. Prov 8. 32. 34 & 29 v. 18. Esa. 56 12. Ap. 16. 15. & 22. v. 7. 4. Jerem. 13. 27 [Hebrew: אוי לך ירושלם] vae tibi Ierusalem, Ezech. 16. 23. Hos. 7. 13. 2. Thess. 1. 9 Jud. 6. 7. 13 quibus etiam per prædicationem Mediatorem patefecit, non ut salutis seu vitæ æternæ participes fiant, ut Lutherani volunt: quia sic fine suo Deus frustraretur; reprobi enim salutis æternæ participes non fiunt, fine autem frustrari quem intendit, impotentis & imprudentis est, quia nemo sanæ mentis eum actioni suæ finem præstituit, quem non assequi præscit, quod de Deo, citra blasphemiam affirmari non potest, sed ut ἀναπολόγητοι reddantur, & justam damnationis suæ causam intelligant. Sic olim Deus, in natura se gentibus patefecit, ut inexcusabiles reddantur, Rom. 1. 20. quæ quidem non omnibus, sed aliquibus tantùm contigit. Multi enim olim reprobi & peccatores mortui sunt, & hodie moriuntur, qui de Jesu nihil audiverunt, qui in remotissimis mundi partibus, vel insulis fuerunt, inter quos ne minimæ auditionis perceptæ de Christo, minima indicia fuêre deprehensa, ut constat ex Americanis, qui ante 130. circiter annos inventi sunt.
units.tr: III. It is declared from the object. For there are those to whom the preaching is directed: either believers, or unbelievers and hypocrites. To believers, whether all together or each one singly, is publicly announced the remission of sins and eternal life, on account of the merit of Jesus apprehended by faith, in the promise of the Gospel (Matt. 9:2; 25:46; Mark 1:4; Luke 5:20; John 3:15-17; 4:13-14; 5:24; 6:40, 47, 50-51, 54; 8:51-52; 10:27-28; 11:26; 1 Tim. 1:16; Jas. 5:15; 1 John 2:24-25; 1 Pet. 1:2-3; Jude 21). Oh how blessed are those, since their sins are forgiven (Ps. 32; Rom. 4:7-9), for they have striven after piety, justice, sincerity (Ps. 106:3; 119:1-2; 128:1; Prov. 8:32, 34; 29:18; Isa. 56:12; Rev. 16:15; 22:7). To unbelievers and hypocrites, on the other hand, a dire and divine retribution is announced, so long as they persevere in their sins (Matt. 5:22, 29-30; Mark 9:92; Luke 12:5; John 20:22-23; compare Isa. 5:18; Jer. 13:27; woe to you, Jerusalem [Hebrew: אוי לך ירושלם] Ezek. 16:23; Hos. 7:13; 2 Thess. 1:9; Jude 6, 7, 13). Through the preaching God has also revealed the Mediator to them, not so that they may become partakers of salvation or eternal life, as the Lutherans want. For thus God would be frustrated in his end: the reprobate do not become partakers of eternal salvation, and to be frustrated in an end one intends is the mark of an impotent and imprudent agent, since no one of sound mind sets himself an end for his action which he foresees he will not attain, and this cannot be affirmed of God without blasphemy. Rather, they are rendered [ἀναπολόγητοι] without excuse, and understand the just cause of their damnation. Thus of old God revealed himself to the nations in nature, so that they would be inexcusable (Rom. 1:20); yet this did not come to all but only to some. For many of the reprobate and dead in sin, both of old and today, have died having heard nothing of Jesus. They were in the most remote parts of the world or on islands, and among them not even the smallest indication of any hearing of Christ has been detected, as is clear from the Americans, who were discovered about 130 years ago.

Quod munus prædicandi, sit honoratissimum, mum, Esa. 52.7 [Hebrew: מַה־נָּאווּ עַל הֶהָרִים רַגְלֵי מְבַשֵּׂר מַשְׁמִיעַ שָׁלוֹם מְבַשֵּׂר־טוֹב] [Hebrew: מַשְׁמִיעַ יְשׁוּעָה אֹמֵר לְצִיּוֹן מָלַךְ אֱלֹהָיִךְ] Rom. 10. v. 15. Act. 13. 2. & 16 v. 10. Rom. 1. v. 1. 1 Cor. 1. v. 1. quàm jucundum, quàm magnificum, aeterni illius legatione fungi fideliter; dicit enim fidelibus suis servis, Euge serve boni, super pauca fuistis fideles, super plura vos constituam, ingredimini in gaudium Domini vestri, Matth. 25. 23.
units.tr: IV. From the properties. 1. That the office of preaching is most honourable (Isa. 52:7 [מַה־נָּאווּ עַל הֶהָרִים רַגְלֵי מְבַשֵּׂר מַשְׁמִיעַ שָׁלוֹם מְבַשֵּׂר־טוֹב מַשְׁמִיעַ יְשׁוּעָה אֹמֵר לְצִיּוֹן מָלַךְ אֱלֹהָיִךְ]: how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who announces peace, who brings good tidings, who announces salvation, who says to Zion, "Your God reigns"; Rom. 10:15 [Ὡς ὡραῖοι οἱ πόδες τῶν εὐαγγελιζομένων εἰρήνην]: how beautiful are the feet of those who bring good things). Hence the Apostle Paul bade the Philippians to receive ministers with all joy and to hold them in honour (Phil. 2:29), since God, King of kings and Lord of lords, has set them apart, separated them, and as it were sent and commissioned them into the possession of that office: [אֲנִי יְהוָה קְרָאתִיךָ בְצֶדֶק וְאַחְזִק בְּיָדֶךָ וְאֶצָּרְךָ וְאֶתְּנְךָ לִבְרִית עָם לְאוֹר גּוֹיִם] "I am the LORD; I have called you in righteousness, and will hold you by the hand, and keep you, and give you as a covenant of the people, as a light of the nations" (Isa. 42:6-7; Acts 13:2; 16:10; Rom. 1:1; 1 Cor. 1:1). How delightful and how glorious it is to serve faithfully in that eternal embassy! For he says to his faithful servants, Well done, good and faithful servant; you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things; enter into the joy of your Lord (Matt. 25:23).

units.tr: II. That it is most difficult, since the ministers must lead the sheep of Jesus by level paths and waters (Ps. 23:3), feed them (Isa. 40:11; Ezek. 34:2, 15; 1 Cor. 9:7), take care that the sheep lack nothing (Ps. 23:1), or fear or be dismayed and pine away (Jer. 23:4); take care that they sleep securely in the woods (Ezek. 34:25); take care that they lie down in a suitable place (Song 1:7), namely in the folds or grassy pastures (Ps. 23:2; Song 2:16; 6:2-3; Jer. 33:12; Ezek. 34:13-15); they must lead them beside gentle waters (Ps. 23:2), to springs or living fountains of waters (Isa. 49:10; Rev. 7:17); they must seek out the straying (Ps. 119:176), gather the scattered (Mic. 2:12; Zeph. 3:19), strengthen the sick (Ezek. 34:16), and lay down their own life for the sheep (John 10:11, 15). Since the office of preaching is so honourable and yet so difficult, we should listen to the word of life proposed by them. For that hearing will be most useful to us, as it contributes great blessings (Gen. 26:4-5; Exod. 15:26; 19:5; 20:6; 23:22, 25; Lev. 20:22; 26:3-5; Deut. 4:4; 28:1, 12; Josh. 7:8; 1 Sam. 12:14; 1 Kings 9:4-5; 2 Kings 10:36; 2 Chron. 7:17; Ps. 85:14-17; Prov. 1:33; Isa. 1:19; Jer. 7:23), so that it is more excellent than sacrifices (1 Sam. 15:22) and more pleasing than the fat of rams (Hos. 6:6; Matt. 9:13; 12:7), inasmuch as it kindles faith in the hearts of the elect, which apprehends the merit of Jesus (Rom. 10:14-15).

units.la: V. Ab effectis; Quia per eam evertitur [Syriac] Regnum SaSatanæ, Luc. 10.18.19. Spectabam, Ἐθεώρουν Satanam, τὸν σατανᾶν ὡς fulgur, ἐκ οὐρανοῦ descendentem, ὡς ἀστραπὴν, ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ πεσόντα. Ἰδε, Ecce δίδωμι ὑμῖν τὴν ἐξουσίαν, dedi vobis potestatem, τὸ πατεῖν ἐπάνω ὄφεων καὶ σκορπίων calcandi supra serpentes, & scorpiones, καὶ ἐπὶ πάσαν τὴν δύναμιν τοῦ ἐχθροῦ καὶ οὐδὲν ὑμᾶς οὐ μὴ ἀδικήσει, & supra omnem vim inimici, & nihil vobis nocebit; expugnatio enim Diaboli, est prædicatio veritatis, sagitta mortifera est in viscera ejus, [Syriac], [Syriac] sermo justitiæ; tanta enim Evangelicæ prædicationis vis, ut brevi tempore, Publicanorum, aut piscatorum opera, in ipsum urbium caput invaserit, ut homines Syri, Romanis Præceptores, atque institutores exstiterint; ut Augustinus, In Præfatione Epistolæ ad Johannem ait, Prædicationem verbi Dei, esse tanquam oleum in flamma in quibusdam, in aliis, tanquam flammam ad fomitem, ut si non ardebat, accedente sermone accendatur.
units.tr: V. From its effects: because through it the kingdom of Satan is overthrown (Luke 10:18, 19). "I beheld Satan [Greek: Ἐθεώρουν τὸν σατανᾶν] as lightning fallen from heaven [Greek: ὡς ἀστραπὴν ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ πεσόντα]. Behold, I give you power [Greek: δίδωμι ὑμῖν τὴν ἐξουσίαν] to tread upon serpents and scorpions [Greek: τὸ πατεῖν ἐπάνω ὄφεων καὶ σκορπίων], and over all the power of the enemy [Greek: καὶ ἐπὶ πάσαν τὴν δύναμιν τοῦ ἐχθροῦ], and nothing shall hurt you [Greek: καὶ οὐδὲν ὑμᾶς οὐ μὴ ἀδικήσει]." For the overthrow of the devil is the preaching of the truth; the deadly arrow is in his bowels [Syriac]; the word of righteousness [Syriac]. So great is the power of evangelical preaching that in a short time the work of tax collectors and fishermen attacked the very head of cities, so that Syrian men became teachers and instructors of the Romans. As Augustine says in the preface to his Epistle to John: the preaching of the word of God is, in some, like oil poured on a flame; in others, like fire set to tinder, so that if it did not burn before, it is kindled when the sermon is added.
