units.la: VI. Ab oppositis. 1. Sunt illi, qui prædicant, & ipsi ne digito quidem attingunt, λέγουσι καὶ οὐ ποιοῦσι, Matth. 23.v.3. Rom. 2.21. de quibus Gregorius Magnus, lib. 8. cap. 26. in Jobum ita loquitur. Proprios favores quærunt, nec proferre alia noverunt, nisi quæ auditorum corda, ad rependendas laudes excitent, non autem ad lacrymas, accendunt. II. Affectus [Syriac] pravi, qui salutiferæ prædicationi repugnant, ut φιλαυτία, quâ illa, quæ carni grata sunt appetimus, Esa. 30.10.11. Amos. 2.12. Curæ, & voluptates hujus seculi, Matth. 13.22. Marc. 4.18.19. Luc. 8.14. Malitia, [Syriac] Jacob 1.21. Quapropter abjectis omnibus sordibus, & excremento malitiæ, cum lenitate, excipite insitum illum sermonem, qui potest servare animas vestras. Levitas animi, tales sunt petrosa terra, qui semen Dei, cum gaudio excipiunt, ortâque persecutione, & compressione, statim offenduntur, Matth. 13.20.21. Matth. 4.15. Luc. 8.13. Securitas, Matth. 13.19. Quia veniens malus spiritus rapit sermonem qui satus est in cordibus ipsorum: hi sunt illi, qui secundum viam semen excipiunt. Luc. 11.32. qui etsi multas audiant conciones: tamen fructum nullum producunt; sicut terra, quæ imbrem imbibit, spinas producit, Heb. 6.18. quæ maledictioni proxima est; exitus enim tendit ad exustionem. Egregie Chrysostomus. In hunc locum loquitur. Timeo, ne quæ hic dicuntur, magis nobis dicantur, quam aliis, semper semper audimus, semper bibimus; sed hamorem statim perdimus, oriente sole, & propterea spinas producimus. Recte tales comparantur piscibus marinis, qui ab ipso ortu in sale nutriuntur, salibus tamen ad condiendum indigent. 3 Calamitates horrendae, persecutiones sanguineae, quae Ministros Ecclesiarum, conticescere cogunt, quare ita conqueritur Jeremias, Lam. 2. 11. Deficiunt lacrymis oculi mei, propter contritionem filiae populi mei, quales in solo meo Natali Pannonio, Hungariâ, praeter propter, ab Anno 1647. ad haec usque tempora grassabantur: ita ut, transverberato Ecclesiae pectore, transfixo pene corde, secto vere jugulo, doctrina de unico Mediatore, Redemtore, Servatore Christo, de unico ejus sacrificio propitiatorio, nox illunis, rarae stellae, & quae rutilabant, errabundae videantur; apparuit enim praesertim in nostro horizonte, caligo illa tristissima, qua mulier illa, purior Ecclesia à Dracone fugata, Apoc. 12. 6. alis, aquilae ingentis subvecta, Deut. 32. 11. eremum petere coacta est, sed Aquila, utique omnipotens Jehova, qui Ecclesiam suam, cum opus, ut pullitiem suam, ad haec usque tempora, servaturus circumtulit, ne aquae, quam Draco evomuit, eam πολαμοφόρηλον ποηίση vorticibus involvat, Apoc. 12. 15. Haec ita esse, mecum loquitur experientia rerum magistra nec non Fratres, in visceribus Jesu dilectissimi, fideles verbi Dei Ministri, quos ad 5. Martii S.N. Anni 1674. ex Hungaria convocando, conticescere coegerunt: Qui proculdubio, eruperunt in haec Gregorii Magni verba: Deo largiente quantum potuimus, coram vobis fratres charissimi, rimati sumus, nemo autem nos reprehendat, si post locutionem suspenderimus, quia uti cernitis nostrae tribulationes excreverunt, undique gladiis circumfusi sumus, versa est in luctum Cithara nostra, organum nostrum in vocem flentium: ) Die 8. Maii Anni 1675. ad Triremes ducendo, crudeliter & tyrannice tractando, e solo delere contenderunt. Sed Jehova, cujus gratia, Die 11. Febr. S.N. Anni 1676. affulsit, & e faucibus leonum, velut alios Danieles, e Fornace Babylonicâ, insolitâ Tyrannide ardente, velut Sidrac, Misac, Abednego socios, liberos esse voluit, ut eorum, & Ecclesiarum Hungaricarum innocentia, vivo quasi in speculo, orbi universo ad stuporem, exponeret, declararet, timoremque Bestiae Apocalypticae incuteret. De quâhaec ingeminare, mihi licitum esto.
units.tr: VI. From the opposites. 1. There are those who preach but do not even touch the thing with a finger: "they say and do not do" [λέγουσι καὶ οὐ ποιοῦσι], Matt. 23:3; Rom. 2:21. Of them Gregory the Great speaks thus in book 8, chapter 26 on Job: They seek their own favour, and know how to utter nothing but what stirs the hearts of their hearers to repay praise, and does not kindle them to tears. II. Evil affections oppose saving preaching, such as self-love [φιλαυτία], by which we desire what is pleasing to the flesh: Isa. 30:10, 11; Amos 2:12. The cares and pleasures of this age: Matt. 13:22; Mark 4:18, 19; Luke 8:14. Malice: James 1:21. Therefore, putting aside all filthiness and overflow of malice, receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls. Fickleness of mind: such people are like stony ground, who receive the seed of God with joy, but when persecution and tribulation arise they are at once offended: Matt. 13:20, 21; Matt. 4:15; Luke 8:13. Complacency: Matt. 13:19, because the evil spirit comes and snatches away the word that was sown in their hearts. These are the ones who receive the seed by the wayside. Luke 11:32: they hear many sermons, yet produce no fruit, like the land that drinks in the rain and produces thorns; Heb. 6:8, which is near to being cursed, for its end is burning. Chrysostom speaks well on this passage: I fear that what is said here is said more to us than to others. We always hear, we always drink, but we at once lose the moisture when the sun rises, and so we produce thorns. Such people are rightly compared to sea fish, which are nourished from their birth in salt, and yet still need salt to be seasoned. 3. Dreadful calamities and bloody persecutions, which compel the ministers of the churches to fall silent. Jeremiah complains thus, Lam. 2:11: My eyes fail with tears, because of the destruction of the daughter of my people. Such things raged in my own native Pannonia, Hungary, more or less from the year 1647 down to these times, so that, with the breast of the Church pierced through, the heart nearly transfixed and the throat truly cut, the doctrine of the one Mediator, Redeemer and Saviour Christ, and of his one propitiatory sacrifice, seems like a moonless night in which the rare stars that were shining wander about. For that most dismal darkness has appeared especially on our horizon, by which that woman, the purer Church, put to flight by the Dragon, Rev. 12:6, borne on the wings of a great eagle, Deut. 32:11, was forced to seek the wilderness. But the Eagle, namely Jehovah almighty, who has carried his Church about until these times as one who would keep it as his own, so that the waters which the Dragon vomited might not sweep her away in whirlpools, Rev. 12:15. That these things are so, experience, the teacher of affairs, speaks with me, and so do my brothers, most beloved in the bowels of Jesus, faithful ministers of the Word of God, whom they forced to fall silent when they summoned them from Hungary on 5 March of the year 1674 (the new style). Doubtless they broke out into these words of Gregory the Great: By God's bounty, as far as we could, we have searched out these things before you, most beloved brothers; but let no one blame us if we break off after speaking, for, as you see, our troubles have increased, we are surrounded on every side by swords, our lyre has turned to mourning, and our organ to the voice of those who weep. On 8 May of the year 1675 they were led off to the galleys, and cruelly and tyrannically treated, and they strove to wipe them out of the land. But Jehovah, whose grace shone forth on 11 February of the year 1676 (new style), and who from the jaws of lions, like other Daniels, and from the Babylonian furnace blazing with unusual tyranny, like Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, willed that they and their companions should be free, so that the innocence of them and of the Hungarian churches might be displayed to the whole world, as though living in a mirror, to its astonishment, and might strike fear into the Beast of the Apocalypse. I may be allowed to repeat these things about it.

units.la: Roma quid insanis, toties quid sanguine gaudes?
units.tr: Rome, why do you rage, why do you so often rejoice in blood?

units.la: Quid geris imbelli spicula tanta manu, &c.
units.tr: Why do you bear such great spears in your unwarlike hand, etc.

units.la: Tu similis colubro, quoties gravis ira venenum, Suscitat, & motâ lumina bile rubent. Sic fremis ut frendens, cùm ferrea vincula mandit, Cerberus & ftigias murmure turbat aquas. Tu fratres in bella vocas in pignora Patres, Nec Jovis Imperium, nec Phlegetonta times.
units.tr: You are like a serpent: whenever grave wrath stirs up its poison, and your eyes glow red with stirred bile. You snarl so that, gnashing, you chew iron chains, and Cerberus and the Stygian waters churn with a murmur. You call brothers to war, fathers to the pledges, and you fear neither the empire of Jove nor Phlegethon.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Secunda clavis œconomiæ Ecclesiasticæ, quæ disciplinâ Ecclesiastica constat, quam παιδείαν seu παιδευσιν Græ. Lat. disciplinam, castigationem, institutionem, vocant, est pædagogia Ecclesiastica, Authoritate verbi Dei instituta, quâ homines, in familiam Christi recepti, ad pietatem diriguntur, & coërcentur, ne quid Christianâ professione indignum committant. Peccantes verò, vel ἀτακτοι redarguuntor, & objurgantor, ut in viam redeant, & juxta doctrinæ Evangelicæ præscriptum, singuli suum officium faciant. Seu, est quâ voluntas Dei, personaliter applicatur censuris, ad illa vitia removenda, quæ cum vera fide & obedientia pugnant, quæ personalis applicatio, est necessaria. (1.) Propter duritiem cordis quæ in plerisque peccatoribus reperitur. (2.) Propter ordinationem Christi, de personali disciplina exercenda quæ quamvis primariò, & directè tendat ad emendationem lapsi, secundariò & indirectè ad emendationem aliorum; est enim veluti frænum, quo retinentur & domantur, qui adversus Christi doctrinam ferociunt: vel tanquam stimulus, quo excitantur parum volutarii, interdùm etiam, veluti paterna ferula, quâ clementer, & pro Spiritu Christi mansuetudine, castigantur qui graviter lapsi sunt, quia ferula, sceptrum disciplinæ est, Ναςδὴς παιδείας ἑςι σκηπτρον, hæc maximâ ex parte, à spirituali jurisdictione pendet, cui subesse omnes debent, siquidem sit optimum sanitatis subsidium, securitatem enim excutit, & ad feriam curam sanitatis excitat. Oh optimum, & immobile ordinis ⟨Hebrew⟩ fundamentum nec non indissolubile, unitatis ⟨Hebrew⟩ vinculum, quæ si non unica, summa & primaria, Ecclesiæ clavis est; sicut nn nulla societas, imò nulla domus, quæ vel modicam familiam habet, contineri in recto statu potest sine disciplina; sic in Ecclesia Dei vivi cujus statum quàm ordinatissimum esse decet, & quemadmodum salutifera Jesu doctrina, anima est Ecclesiæ: sic disciplina pro nervis est: qua fit ut membra corporis suo quoque loco cohæreant, qui ergò vel impediunt restictionem ejus, vel è medio sublatam cupiunt, sive hoc faciant data opera, sive per incogitantiam, extremam certè Ecclesiæ dissipationem quærunt, quid enim futurum est, si unicuique liceat, quod libuerit? quum ergò cernamus, horrendæ vastitatis in Ecclesia imminere initia, ex eo quod nulla cura, nulla ferula, nullum frenum, nulla ratio continendi populi, opus esse remedio, necessitas ipsa clamat, pleno gutture, hoc unicum est remedium, quod & Christus Dominus præcepit, Matth. 16. 19. & 18. 18. Joh. 20. 23. & semper usitatum inter pios fuit.
units.tr: The second key of the economy of the Church, which consists in church discipline (which the Greeks call paideian or paideusin, and the Latins disciplina, castigatio, or institutio), is the pedagogy of the Church, instituted by the authority of God's Word. By it, people received into the family of Christ are guided toward godliness and restrained, so that they do nothing unworthy of their Christian profession. Those who sin, or who are disorderly (ataktoi), are rebuked and reproved, so that they return to the right way and each performs his duty according to the prescription of the Gospel doctrine. Or, it is the means by which the will of God is applied personally through censures to remove those vices which are opposed to true faith and obedience. This personal application is necessary: (1) because of the hardness of heart found in most sinners; (2) because of Christ's ordinance concerning the personal exercise of discipline. Although this discipline aims primarily and directly at the amendment of the fallen person, it aims secondarily and indirectly at the amendment of others. It is like a bridle, by which those who rage against Christ's doctrine are held back and tamed, or like a goad, by which those who are rather unwilling are stirred up; sometimes it is also like a father's rod, with which those who have fallen grievously are chastised gently and in the spirit of Christ's meekness. For the rod is the sceptre of discipline [rhabdos paideias estin skeptron]. This discipline depends for the most part on spiritual jurisdiction, to which all ought to be subject, since it is the best aid to health: it shakes off complacency and arouses a wakeful care for health. O the best and immovable foundation of order, and also the indissoluble bond of unity [Hebrew]! If it is not the only key, it is the chief and first key of the Church. Just as no society, indeed no household, even a very small family, can be kept in good order without discipline, so in the Church of the living God, whose state ought to be as orderly as possible, discipline is to the Church what the nerves are to the body, while the saving doctrine of Jesus is its soul. Hence the members of the body cohere each in its place. Those, then, who hinder its restraint, or who desire it removed altogether, whether they do so deliberately or through thoughtlessness, are seeking the utter dissipation of the Church. For what will become of things if each may do whatever he pleases? Since we see the beginnings of a dreadful devastation threatening the Church, because there is no care, no rod, no bridle, and no means of restraining the people, necessity itself cries out with full throat that a remedy is needed. This is the only remedy, which Christ the Lord also commanded (Matt. 16:19; 18:18; John 20:23), and it has always been in use among the godly.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Hæc Secunda clavis, explicatur ab objecto circa quod. Duplex autem est objectum. Personale & Reale; Illud non bruta animantia, mortui, absentes, ignoti, non etiam pœnitus extranei, cujusmodi sunt hodie Judæi, Turcæ: nec etiam schismatici, Hæretici, & qui prorsus ab Ecclesia Christiana, discessum, recesserunt, vel nunquam veræ Ecclesiæ sese adjunxerunt: ut Pontificii volunt, sed ii duntaxat, qui adhuc in sinu Ecclesiæ versantur seu frater peccans, Matth. 18. 15. 1. Cor. 5. v. 11. Ejusdem professionis collega, Lev. 21. 10. 1. Reg. 13. 30. 1. Chron. 16 37. 38. 39. 2. Chron. 35. 15. Esd. 3. 2. 9. & 6. v. 26. & 7. v. 18. Actor. 21. 20 liquidem ille debet subesse huic curatelæ, qui frater censeri vult, ne exceptis quidem magnatibus. Hinc Origenes homilia 21. in su: inquit. Quia non possumus, ex Ierusalem omnes Iebusæos ejicere, ejiciamus scilicet eos, quos possumus, quorum peccata manifesta sunt, ubi enim peccatum non est manifestum, neminem de Ecclesia ejicere possumus, Matth. 23. 8. Col. 3. 11. 2. Pet. 1. v. 1c. Ergo Pontifex Romanus, instar ovis incustoditæ aberrat, quia Pont. hujus censuræ immunem faciunt, & extra limen Ecclesiæ esse asserunt, ignorantes, aut perverse detorquentes illud, qui Ecclesiam Matrem non habet in terris, ille Deum Patrem non habet in cœlis. Reale tum Doctrina, tum vita labes, illud est error in Doctrina seu dogmate, qui vel ex sola simplici ignorantia, vel simul ex improbitate oritur: si autem à recepta sana doctrina ita recedatur, ut contemtu Dei, & Ecclesiæ ipsius indicio, sententia, obstinatè & pertinaciter defendatur, & Ecclesiæ Concordia violetur, Hæresis dicitur. Illud est peccatum, dictum aut factum, quo proximus læsus est, Matt. 18. 15. Rom. 16. 17. Precor autem vos Fratres, ut observetis, dissidiorum, & offendiculorum auctores, παρὰ τὴν διδαχὴν. Præter doctrinam, ἣν ὑμεῖς ἐμάθετε, quam, vos didicistis: Καὶ exἐκκλίνατε ἀπ᾽ αὐτῶν, & declinate ab eis, 1. Cor. 5. 11. 1. Tim. 1. 20. Tit. 3. 10. 11. 2. Joh. 1. 10. si quis venerit ad vos, καὶ ταύτην τὴν διδαχὴν, οὐ φέρει, Et hanc doctrinam non adfert, μὴ λαμβάνετε αὐτὸν εἰς οἰκίαν ne accipite eum in domum, καὶ χαίρειν αὐτῷ μὴ λέγετε, nec ave ei dicite, 3. Joh. v. 10. quorum lucerna extinguetur, & superveniet interitus eorum, Job. 21. 17. Psal. 37. 28. Semen [Hebrew] corum exscindetur, Pro. 2. 22. & 4. v. 19. & 10. v. 25. 27. & 15. v. 10. & 12. 7. & 13. 9. & 20. v. 26. & 24. v. 16. 20. Esa. 57. 21. Jerem. 25. 31. Ezech. 33. v. 8. Mich. 6. 10. Sopho. 1. 3. Mal 4. 3. 1. Pet. 4. 18. Jud. v. 15. Errant ergo Remonstrantes de Haeresi dubitantes, cum doctrinae [Arabic] corruptio ut venenum à Jesu separat, jussit etiam Christus vitari, Matth. 16. v. 6. 12.
units.tr: This second key is explained by its object, with which it is concerned. The object is twofold: personal and real. The personal object is not brute animals, the dead, the absent, the unknown, nor even those who are wholly outside, such as today the Jews and Turks; nor schismatics and heretics, nor those who have utterly departed from the Christian Church or never joined themselves to the true Church, as the Papists want. Rather, it is only those who still dwell within the bosom of the Church: a brother who sins (Matt. 18:15), (1 Cor. 5:11), a fellow of the same profession (Lev. 21:10; 1 Kings 13:30; 1 Chron. 16:37-39; 2 Chron. 35:15; Ezra 3:2, 9; 6:26; 7:18; Acts 21:20). Certainly whoever wishes to be counted a brother must be subject to this oversight, not even excepting the great men. Hence Origen, homily 21 on Joshua, says: Because we cannot cast all the Jebusites out of Jerusalem, let us cast out at least those whom we can, whose sins are manifest; for where sin is not manifest, we cannot cast anyone out of the Church. (Matt. 23:8; Col. 3:11; 2 Pet. 1:1.) Therefore the Roman Pontiff goes astray like a sheep left unguarded, because the Pontiffs make this censure void for some and assert that they are outside the threshold of the Church. They are ignorant of, or wrongly twist, the saying that he who does not have the Church as mother on earth does not have God as Father in heaven. The real object is the blemish of doctrine and of life. The blemish of doctrine is error in teaching or dogma, which arises either from simple ignorance alone or at the same time from wickedness. But if one departs from the received sound doctrine in such a way that, in contempt of God and of the Church's own judgment, an opinion is stubbornly and obstinately defended, and the concord of the Church is violated, it is called heresy. The blemish of life is a sin, a word or deed by which a neighbour is injured (Matt. 18:15; Rom. 16:17). "I beseech you, brethren, mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned" [para tēn didachēn hēn hymeis emathete], "and avoid them" [kai ekklinate ap' auton] (1 Cor. 5:11; 1 Tim. 1:20; Titus 3:10-11; 2 John 10). "If there come any unto you and bring not this doctrine" [kai tautēn tēn didachēn ou pherei], "receive him not into your house" [mē lambanete auton eis oikian], "neither bid him God speed" [kai chairein autō mē legete] (3 John 10). "Their lamp shall be put out, and their destruction shall come upon them" (Job 21:17; Ps. 37:28). "Their seed shall be cut off" [Hebrew] (Prov. 2:22; 4:19; 10:25, 27; 15:10; 12:7; 13:9; 20:26; 24:16, 20; Isa. 57:21; Jer. 25:31; Ezek. 33:8; Mic. 6:10; Zeph. 1:3; Mal. 4:3; 1 Pet. 4:18; Jude 15). The Remonstrants therefore err who doubt whether this is a matter of heresy, since, as the corruption of doctrine separates from Jesus like poison, [Arabic word] Christ also commanded that it be avoided (Matt. 16:6, 12).

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Disciplinae Ecclesiasticae, duae sunt partes, Correptio fraterna & Excommunicatio. Illa est censura, ad peccati modum, & peccatoris vel obstinati, vel verè confitentis, & resipiscentiam profitentis, ad aedificationem accommodata, quae aliquoties debet repeti, non enim consistit vel tantum, vel praecipuè in Excommunicationum & Anathematum fulmine, sed potissimum in Christianâ correptione, cui salutari medelae si locum dederit auscultando, seu obtemperando admonitionibus tuis: (auscultare enim est obtemperare, Gen. 37. 27. Exod. 7. 4. 13. 16. 22. Deut. 13. 8. Jud. 2. 17. 1. Sam. 2. 25. 2. Reg. 14. 11. 2. Chron. 25. 20: Estr. 3. 4. Prov. 5. 7. & ne recedatis ab eloquiis oris mei, Jer. 7. 27. Eze. 3. 6. 7. Philem. v. 21.) Lucratus es ipsum, ut ex coetu ne ejiciatur. Contra verò si non auscultaverit, seu mandata Dei, & admonitiones ejus, ex S. Sacra petitas (si quidem illinc debent peti, non ex placitis hominum; secus enim conscientias non penetrant, quoniam verbum Dei, verae sapientiae, Psal. 119. 98. 99. 100. omnisque consolationis, ibidem v. 25. 28. 31. 40. 50. Rom. 15. 4. fons & scaturigo, denique nulli non aetati utile, Psal. 1. 2. Rom. 1. 16. pueris, & senibus, Deut. 6. v. 7. 2. Tim. 3. 15. Psal. 119. v. 9. 100. Sapientibus & insipientibus, Rom. 1. 14. Pastoribus & auditoribus, 1. Tim. 4. 16. 2. Tim. 4. 16. Regibus & Subditis, Deut. 17. 18. 19. 1. Sam. 12. v. 15. Contemserit, rejecerit, cum non auscultare, sit ejus mandata contemnere, rejicere, Exod. 7. 16. Lev. 26. 14. 18. Deut. 30: 17. 2. Reg. 17. 14. Esa. 42. 23. Jerem. 12. 17. Ezech. 3. 7. Hos. 9. 17. Mic. 5. 15. dic Ecclesiae, si nec Ecclesiam audiverit ut tabidum membrum resecetur, Matth. 10. 18.
units.tr: The discipline of the Church has two parts: fraternal correction and excommunication. The former is a censure suited to the kind of sin and to the sinner, whether he is obstinate or truly confesses and professes repentance, and it is intended for edification. It may need to be repeated several times. It does not consist only, or chiefly, in the thunderbolt of excommunications and anathemas, but above all in Christian correction. If the sinner gives place to this healing remedy by listening, that is, by obeying your admonitions (for to listen is to obey: Gen. 37:27; Exod. 7:4, 13, 16, 22; Deut. 13:8; Judg. 2:17; 1 Sam. 2:25; 2 Kings 14:11; 2 Chron. 25:20; Esther 3:4; Prov. 5:7; "and do not depart from the words of my mouth," Jer. 7:27; Ezek. 3:6, 7; Philem. 21), then "you have gained him, so that he is not cast out of the assembly" (Matt. 18:15). On the other hand, if he does not listen, that is, does not heed the commands of God and his admonitions drawn from Holy Scripture (and they must indeed be drawn from there, not from the opinions of men, for otherwise they do not reach the conscience, since the Word of God is the source and spring of true wisdom, Ps. 119:98–100, and of all consolation, ibid. vv. 25, 28, 31, 40, 50; Rom. 15:4; and it is useful at every age, Ps. 1:2; Rom. 1:16, for children and for the aged, Deut. 6:7; 2 Tim. 3:15; Ps. 119:9, 100; for the wise and the foolish, Rom. 1:14; for ministers and hearers, 1 Tim. 4:16; 2 Tim. 4:16; for kings and subjects, Deut. 17:18, 19; 1 Sam. 12:15), then to refuse to listen is to despise and reject his commands (Exod. 7:16; Lev. 26:14, 18; Deut. 30:17; 2 Kings 17:14; Isa. 42:23; Jer. 12:17; Ezek. 3:7; Hos. 9:17; Mic. 5:15), and "tell it to the Church"; and if he will not hear the Church either, he is to be cut off like a diseased member (Matt. 18:17).

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Fraternam hanc admonitionem, à quinque proprietatibus, ex S.Sacra petitis, explicamus, 1. Quod Commendetur, ἐν γραφαῖς ἁγίαις. Lev.19.17.18. Ne odio habeas, לֹא תִשְׂנָא fratrem tuum, אָחִיךָ in corde tuo, בְּלִבָּבְךָ corripiendo corripies, הוֹכֵחַ תּוֹכִיחַ proximum tuum, אֶת־עֲמִיתֶךָ & ne feras, וְלֹא תִשָּׂא super illo peccatum, עָלָיו חֵטְא Prov.1.22.23. תָּשֵׁבוּ לְתוֹכַחְתִּי convertimini ad increpationem meam, & cap.9. v.7.8. תוֹכַח. increpa sapientem amabit te, & cap.10.v.17. & 17.v.32. אֹהֵב מוּסָר Diligens correctionem, diligens scientiam, & 13.v.1. & 15.v.31. & 17.v.10. & 24.v.25.&25.v.12.& 27.v.5.& 28.v.23.Matth.18.15.Luc.17.3. Si peccaverit frater tuus, ἐπιτίμησον αὐτῷ, increpa eum, Gal.2.11.&6.v.1. 1.Thess.5.14. 1.Tim.5.v.1. 20.τὰς ἁμαρτάνοντας, peccantes, ἐνώπιον πάντων, coram omnibus, ἔλεγχε argue, 2.Tim.2.25. Exemplum [Hebrew]. In Loto, Gen. 19.v.7.
units.tr: We explain this fraternal admonition under five properties, drawn from Holy Scripture. 1. That it is commended in the holy Scriptures [ἐν γραφαῖς ἁγίαις] (Lev. 19:17, 18): "You shall not hate your brother [לֹא תִשְׂנָא אָחִיךָ] in your heart [בְּלִבָּבְךָ]; you shall surely rebuke [הוֹכֵחַ תּוֹכִיחַ] your neighbour [אֶת־עֲמִיתֶךָ], and you shall not bear sin upon him [וְלֹא תִשָּׂא עָלָיו חֵטְא]." Prov. 1:22, 23: "Turn at my reproof [תָּשֵׁבוּ לְתוֹכַחְתִּי]"; and ch. 9:7, 8: "Rebuke [תוֹכַח] a scoffer, and he will hate you; rebuke a wise man, and he will love you." Also ch. 10:17; ch. 17:32; "loves correction [אֹהֵב מוּסָר]"; "loves knowledge"; and ch. 13:1; 15:31; 17:10; 24:25; 25:12; 27:5; 28:23. Matt. 18:15; Luke 17:3: "If your brother sins, rebuke him [ἐπιτίμησον αὐτῷ]." Gal. 2:11; 6:1; 1 Thess. 5:14; 1 Tim. 5:1, 20: "those who sin [τὰς ἁμαρτάνοντας], in the sight of all [ἐνώπιον πάντων]." 2 Tim. 2:25: "convict [ἔλεγχε], argue." Examples: Hebrew [Hebrew]. In Lot, Gen. 19:7: "I beg you, brothers, do not do wrong."

units.la: Ne quaso fratres faciatis malum. In Rubeno, qui fratres Josephum occidere volentes, ita increpat, Gen.37.22. ne effundatis sanguinem, ne immittite manum in eum. In Moise, Exod.2.13. Acto.7.26. In Ietrone, Exod.18.13.14. In Israelitis, Jud.20.v.12. In Jonathane, 1.Sam.19.4.5.6. & 20.v.32. In Davide, 1.Sam.24.15.16. In Abigail, 1.Sam.25.37. In Abnero, 2.Sam.2.21.22. In Natane, Davidem Regem increpante, 2.Sam.12.1.7. In Daniele, Baltasarum Regem Babyloniæ objurgante, Dan.5.22.23. In Johanne Baptista, qui progenies viperarum arguebat, Matt.3.7. In Christo, Matth.17.18. In Petro, Acto.3.12. In Paulo, Acto.13.10. Gal.3.1.2.Thess.3.15.
units.tr: Reuben, who, wanting his brothers to kill Joseph, rebukes them thus: Gen. 37:22: "Do not shed blood, do not lay a hand on him." In Moses, Exod. 2:13; Acts 7:26. In Jethro, Exod. 18:13, 14. In the Israelites, Judg. 20:12. In Jonathan, 1 Sam. 19:4–6; and 20:32. In David, 1 Sam. 24:15, 16. In Abigail, 1 Sam. 25:37. In Abner, 2 Sam. 2:21, 22. In Nathan, rebuking King David, 2 Sam. 12:1, 7. In Daniel, rebuking Belshazzar, King of Babylon, Dan. 5:22, 23. In John the Baptist, who called the Pharisees a brood of vipers, Matt. 3:7. In Christ, Matt. 17:18. In Peter, Acts 3:12. In Paul, Acts 13:10; Gal. 3:1; 2 Thess. 3:15.

units.la: II. Quòd sit summæ utilitatis Ecclesiæ in his terris militantis, & membrorum ejus, Prov.19.25.&25.v.11.&27.v.5. melior est correptio manifesta, amore occulto, Eccl.7.5. III. Quòd non sit temerè adhibenda, sine vera & infallibili causa, non ad aspectum oculorum judicemus, neque ad aurium auditum corripiamus, sit ergo regula Christus Dominus nobis, qui non judicabit [Hebrew] ad visum oculorum [Hebrew] neque ad auditum aurium suarum arguet. IV. Quod aquo animo sit suscipienda, nam honorabitur ille qui auscultat correptioni, Prov.13.8.&maximopere ille animam suam diligere dicitur: Contra, qui contemnit correptionem, odit animam suam, Prov.15.32. Vrit increpatio prudentem, Prov.17.10.Psal.141.5. David dicit increpatio justi [Hebrew] unguentum est praestantissimum. V. Quòd hujus contemptus sit venenatus & noxius, xius valdè,Prov.9.17. & 12.1. & 13.v.18. & 15.v.11.12. 32.&29. v.1. quàm peccaminosus derisor rejicit ; sed sapiens æquo animo suscipit,Prov.9.8. ne corripito derisorem, ut non odio habeat te, corripe sapientem, amabit te.
units.tr: II. That it is of the greatest usefulness to the Church militant on this earth, and to its members (Prov. 19:25; 25:11; 27:5): "Open rebuke is better than secret love" (Eccl. 7:5). III. That it is not to be applied rashly, without a true and infallible cause: "He shall not judge by the sight of his eyes, nor reprove after the hearing of his ears" (Isa. 11:3). Christ the Lord is therefore our rule, who "shall not judge [לֹא־לְמַרְאֵה עֵינָיו ... ] by the sight of his eyes, nor reprove by the hearing of his ears." IV. That it is to be received with an even mind: for he who listens to correction is said to be honoured and to love his own soul most of all (Prov. 13:8); on the contrary, he who despises correction hates his own soul (Prov. 15:32). "Rebuke goes deeper into a wise man than a hundred blows" (Prov. 17:10; Ps. 141:5). David says: "the rebuke of the righteous is the finest ointment." V. That the contempt of it is poisonous and harmful, as the sinful scoffer rejects it, but the wise man receives it with an even mind (Prov. 9:17; 12:1; 13:18; 15:11, 12, 32; 29:1). Prov. 9:8: "Do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you; rebuke a wise man, and he will love you."

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Correptio,seu תוכחה. 2.Reg.19.3. Psal.149.7. Est Privata vel Publica. Hæc est quæ non unum,vel alterum testem habet,& coram uno aut altero fit ; sed palam & cum totius Ecclesiæ offensione designatur. Privata,seu occulta voco,non quæ homines prorsus latent, qualia sunt hypocritarum: (nàm illa sub Censurâ Ecclesiæ non sunt :) Sed medii generis, quæ scil: testibus non carent, neque tamen sunt publica.Prima species non requirit gradus,nec secunda, nisi accedat contumacia, hæc humanitas, nisi tàm privatim, quàm communiter servetur,periculum est ne ex disciplina, mox devenia-mus ad carnificinam ; non enim omnes qui peccant,statim habendi sunt pro Ethnicis & Publicanis, seu alienis à fide,Matt. 18.15. 16.17. Si enim hoc faceremus,judicaremus proximum,temerè & malignè damnaremus,atque adeò de eo,deque dictis ejus,& factis male sentiremus interpretantes ea in malam partem,quojudicio interdixit Christus Dominus,Matt.12.47. Ne judicetis,hoc est ne sitis rigidi censores proximi,atque adeò ne reprehendatis studio infamandi & comparandi vobis,ex eorum reprehensione & damnatione,opinionem probitatis,aut capiendi oblectationem ex eorum infamia ; sed studio emendandi agatis circa proximum,Matth.7.1. Luc.6.37. & non judicabimini,ne condemnetis,& non condemnabimini, observemus ergo,tres à Christo Domino Matt.18.v.15.16. 17. præscriptos gradus,juxta quos incedere nobis sit perpetuum & necessarium.
units.tr: Correction, or tokhachah [תוכחה], 2 Kings 19.3; Psalm 149.7. It is either private or public. The public kind is the one that does not rest on one or two witnesses, but takes place openly, in front of others, and causes offence to the whole Church. I call it private or hidden, not in the sense of wrongs that men conceal entirely, such as those of hypocrites (for those do not fall under the censure of the Church), but of a middle kind, which indeed have witnesses but are not public. The first kind does not require steps, nor does the second, unless obstinacy is added. This gentleness must be observed as much in private as in public, or there is a danger that from discipline we will soon come to the executioner's block. For not all who sin are at once to be held as heathens and tax-collectors, that is, strangers to the faith (Matt. 18.15-17). If we did this, we would judge our neighbour rashly and condemn him maliciously, and so think ill of him, his words and his deeds, interpreting them in the worst sense. Christ the Lord forbade this kind of judgment (Matt. 12.47): Judge not, that is, do not be harsh censors of your neighbour, and do not rebuke him in order to defame him, or to win for yourselves a reputation for uprightness from his reproof and condemnation, or to take pleasure from his infamy; but act with zeal for amending your neighbour (Matt. 7.1; Luke 6.37), and you will not be judged, that is, do not condemn, and you will not be condemned. Let us therefore observe the three steps prescribed by Christ the Lord (Matt. 18.15-17), by which our progress must always and necessarily proceed.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: I. Gradus,Matt.18.v.15.Exprimitur,si peccaverit in te frater,(quàm particulam aliter, nisi contentiosus esse velis,accipere non potes,quàm sub tua conscientia,ita ut non sint plures conscii :) seu, quocunque modo læserit & quocunque modo offenderit,vide simile.1.Sam.19.4. Ubi Jonatan ad Patrem suum Saulem pro Davide interpellans,sic loquitur, אל יחטא המלך בעבדו בדויד ne peccet Rex in vum suum Davidem,quasi diceret,noli ei malefacere,noli malum, vel mortem ei machinari, לא חטא לך כילא,quia non peccavit in te,non læsit te nullâ in re offendit te. Sic Ruben,Gen.22.v.22, increpans fratres suos אל תחטאו בילד,ne peccetis in puerum, h.e. nolite lædere, re & interficere. Sic Salamon in dedicatione templi Hierosolimi-tani את אשר יחטא איש לרעהו , cum quis peccaverit in proximum suum, seu cum aliquâ ratione læserit & offenderit re vel facto, exaudi: versu eodem dicit jam, argue eum inter te & ipsum solum, non enim in levioribus peccatis adhibenda tanta severitas, quanta in gravioribus; sed sufficit verborum castigatio, eaque ܠܥܒܕܘ lenis & paterna, quæ non exasperat peccatorem, ne confundatur; sed debet ad se ipsum deducere; ut ܐܢܫܐ magis gaudeat se correctum, quàm tristatum, siquidem cum spiritu mansuetudinis conjuncta esse debet, quemadmodum præcipit Divus Paulus, 2. Cor. 2. 7. ne absorbeatur in tristitia is, in quem animadvertitur; sic enim ex remedio exitium fieret, ex quo patet. 1. Multa facienda esse cum proximo, ut lucri fiat. II. Dùm monetur peccator, & arguitur consulendum est ipsius existimationi apud alios, ne pro studio ædificandi invalescat φιδυμισμὸς & καταλαλιὰ, susurratio & objurgatio, 1. Pet. 2. 1. Jac. 4. 11. & Extensio digiti, Esa. 58. 9. III. Justum & debitum est, obtemperanti condonare, Luc. 17. 3. 4. 2. Cor. 2. 7. 8. 10. ad quæ verba Chrysostomus hom. 4. ait, Vides quo pacto posteriores partes sibi tribuit: illos videlicet duces atque auspices se in comitem duntaxat ostendens. Ut acerbatus animus mitigetur, durus ac pertinax emolliatur. Flagitiis autem atrociori opus est remedio; neque enim satis est, si facinore mali exempli edito, graviter Ecclesiam læserit ut verbis tantum castigetur; sed privari ad tempus communione cœnæ debet, donec resipiscentiæ suæ fidem fecerit, 1. Cor. 5. 5. Ut recte præcipiunt Hebræi teste Cicerone. Habenda ratio & diligentia est, ut primum monitio acerbitate, deinde objurgatio contumelia careat. Eodem modo habetur in libro Musar: CCXXI. Qui arguit socium suum, debet primum hoc facere placide, inter se & ipsum, verbis mollibus, ita ut non pudefaciat eum; si resipuerit bene est: Sin: debet eum acriter arguere, & pudefacere inter se & ipsum, si non resipuerit, debet adhibere socios, ipsumque coram illis pudore afficere: si nec hoc modo quicquam proficit, debet eum pudefacere coram multis, ejusque delictum publicare, nam certè detegendi sunt hypocritæ. Drusius, ἐὰν σε ἀκούσῃ, ἐκέρδησας τὸν ἀδελφόν σε. Si te audiverit, lucratus es fratrem tuum: non enim dicit Christus Dominus, tibi bene consuluisti, sed fratri, id enim præcipuè positum nobis esse debet læsis, nàm nostra, aut res aut existimatio, agitur temporaria illius salus æterna, κερδαίνῃν, est ad bobonam frugem convertere, revocare, ac proinde in salutis viam reducere, 1. Cor. 9.19. Paulus servus factus, ut plures lucrifaceret, exlegibus ut lex ut lucrifaceret exleges v.21. Factus est Ioo infirmus, ut firmus, ut infirmos lucrifaceret, v. 22. omnibus factus est omnia, ut omnino aliquos servaret, 1. Pet. 3.1. Fatemur non pastores tantum debere in hanc partem incumbere, ne quid in Ecclesia vitii remaneat; sed unicuique eo annitendum pro sua virili; omnes enim tenentur aliquomodo significare scandalum admissum, ex conscientia erga Deum serio displicere, Eph. 5.11. charitas enim & Z elus Dei hoc postulat, nec dissimulent, quia qui malos monere, arguere, corrigere negligit, etiam si non favet iis, coram Deo reum esse; misericorditer igitur corripiat, quod potest: quod autem non potest, patienter ferat, & cum dilectione gemat, & lugeat; nam praeceptum peccantem fratrem admonendi solenniter, tum obstringit, cum spes est aliqua vel mediate, vel immediate ad scandalum tollendum valitura.
units.tr: I. The step (Matt. 18.15) is expressed in the words if your brother sin against you (which particle you cannot understand otherwise, unless you wish to be contentious, than as applying to what is within your own knowledge, so that there are not several witnesses), or, in whatever way he has harmed you and in whatever way he has offended you. Compare a similar passage, 1 Sam. 19.4, where Jonathan, pleading for David with his father Saul, speaks thus: let not the king sin against his servant David [אל יחטא המלך בעבדו בדויד], as if he said: do not do him any harm, do not plot evil or death against him; for he has not sinned against you [לא חטא לך כי לא], that is, he has not harmed you or offended you in any matter. So Reuben, Gen. 22.22, rebuking his brothers: do not sin against the boy [אל תחטאו בילד], that is, do not injure him in word or deed. So Solomon at the dedication of the temple of Jerusalem: when someone sins against his neighbour [את אשר יחטא איש לרעהו], that is, when someone has harmed and offended in some way by word or deed, hear; and in the same verse he says, reprove him between you and him alone. For in lesser sins so great a severity is not to be applied as in graver ones; a rebuke in words is enough, and that gentle and fatherly, which does not exasperate the sinner, so that he is not confounded, but leads him back into himself, so that he rejoices more to be corrected than to be saddened. For it must be joined with a spirit of gentleness, as the Divine Paul commands (2 Cor. 2.7): lest such a one be swallowed up by sadness; for otherwise the remedy would become ruin. From this it is clear: 1. Much must be done with one's neighbour so that he may be gained. II. While a sinner is being admonished and reproved, care must be taken of his reputation among others, lest, out of zeal for building up, whispering [ψιθυρισμός] and backbiting [καταλαλιά] grow strong (1 Pet. 2.1; Jas. 4.11), and the pointing of the finger (Isa. 58.9). III. It is right and fitting to forgive one who obeys (Luke 17.3-4; 2 Cor. 2.7-8, 10). On these words Chrysostom, in homily 4, says: See how he assigns to himself the lesser part, showing himself merely as a companion, when he might have been the leader and guide, so that the embittered spirit may be softened and the hard and stubborn may be made gentle. But more atrocious crimes require a stronger remedy. It is not enough, if a man, by committing a deed of bad example, has grievously harmed the Church, that he be rebuked only in words; he must be deprived for a time of communion in the Lord's Supper until he has given proof of his repentance (1 Cor. 5.5). This is rightly prescribed by the Hebrews, as Cicero testifies: Care and diligence must be taken that the admonition at first be free of harshness, and then that the rebuke be free of insult. The same is found in the book Musar, CCXXI: He who reproves his companion must first do this quietly, between himself and him, with soft words, so that he does not shame him; if he repents, it is well. If not, he must reprove him sharply and shame him between himself and him. If he still does not repent, he must bring in companions and bring him to shame in their presence. If even this achieves nothing, he must shame him before many and make his offence public, for hypocrites must certainly be exposed. Drusius: if he hears you, you have gained your brother [ἐὰν σου ἀκούσῃ, ἐκέρδησας τὸν ἀδελφόν σου]. For Christ the Lord does not say, you have done well for yourself, but for your brother; for this above all ought to be set before us when we have been wronged. Our own goods or reputation are at stake, but his eternal salvation is at stake too, and to gain [κερδαίνειν] means to turn him to good fruit, to call him back, and thus to lead him into the way of salvation (1 Cor. 9.19-22): Paul, made a slave to all, that he might gain more; to those without law, as though without law, that he might gain those without law; made weak to the weak, that he might gain the weak; made all things to all men, that he might by all means save some. We grant that not only ministers ought to take this task upon themselves, lest any fault remain in the Church; each one must strive for it according to his strength. For all are bound in some way to show that a scandal has been committed, to be seriously displeased in conscience before God (Eph. 5.11). For love and the zeal of God demand this, and they should not dissemble, because whoever neglects to admonish, reprove and correct the wicked is guilty before God, even if he does not favour them. Let him therefore rebuke mercifully what he can; what he cannot, let him bear patiently, and mourn and grieve with love. For the precept to admonish a sinning brother solemnly binds us only when there is some hope that it may serve, either directly or indirectly, to remove the scandal.

units.la: II. Gradus correctionis v. 16. habetur. Ἐὰν δὲ μὴ ἀκούσῃ, παρακάλεσε μετὰ σοῦ ἔτι ἕνα ἢ δύο. Sin vero te non audiverit, adhibe adhuc unum vel duos: ἵνα ἐπὶ στόματος δύο μαρτύρων ἢ τριῶν σταθῇ πᾶν ῥῆμα. Ut in ore duorum aut trium testium stet omne verbum, non enim post admonitionem privatam rejectam statim ad Ecclesiam debet deferri, sed unum aut duos assumere debemus, & coram illis admonitionem urgere, quia eorum testimonio adhibita monitio confirmatur, vel apud fratrem errantem, vel apud Ecclesiam postea correcturam: admonuisse autem fratrem peccantem privatim semel, coram testibus semel non sufficit; sed eo usque (cum patientia & longanimitate) debet admonere, dum vel poenitentiam, vel contumaciam suam fecerit manifestam: si te audiverit, si te non audiverit, si neglexerit eos audire, Matth. 16. v. 15. 16. 17. quae verba sunt legis ex Deut. 19.15. ex versione LXX. interpretum, ubi sapienter exigit lex Divina, testes in quacunque causa binos, aut ternos, primum rejiciens testimonia singularia, deinde ostendens eam posse esse alicujus viri famam, ut facile non uni tantum; sed & duobus testibus fit ἰσοταλαντ, non enim testis unus, in judicio sufficit, unde teste uno apud Judaeos in V. T. nemo damnabatur, sed tribus ad minimum aut duobus erat opus, hinc Hieronymus l. 2. Apollo: adv: Ruffinum; (Unico testi nec Catoni creditum est:) Num. 35. v. 30. Testis unus non potest testari contra aliquem ut moriatur, Deut. 17. Deut. 17.6.7. & 19.v. 15. & 30.v.19. Josu.24. 22. Rut.4.9.10.11. Job.10.17. Psal.27.12.& 35.v.11. Esa.10.12.& 44.v.8.9. Jer.32. v.10.12.25. Dan.13.40. Matth. 18.16.& 26.v.60.65. Marc.14.63. Luc.24.48. Act.1.8. 2. Cor. 13.1. 1. Tim. 5.19. & 6.v.12. Heb. 10.28. Jezabel etiam, Achabi Regis Israel Uxor, duos testes jubet Naboto collocari, ut arguant eum, 1.Reg.21.10. dicendo maledixi-sti Deo & Regi : per se patet nos non docere his verbis, eo ipso quod duo aut tres, vel plures testantur de re aliqua, sit illico verum, ipsique testes falsi censeri non possunt, ac mendaces, ita ut non opus hic allegorizare, quod facere cum Augustino necessarium duximus, qui tractat: 36. in Johan: ita loquitur: In ore duorum aut trium testium stabit omne verbum, veritas quaeritur per duos testes, ita plane se habet humani generis consuetudo; sed tamen fieri potest, ut & duo mentiantur. Susanna duobus falsis testibus urgebatur, num quid, quia duo erant, ideo falsi testes non erant, de duobus aut de tribus quaeritur. Universus populus mentitus est contra Christum, si ergo populus constans ex magna hominum multitudine falsus testis inventus est, quomodo accipiendum est, in ore duorum aut trium testium stabit omne verbum. Nisi hoc modo mysterium Trinitatis commendatum est, in qua est perpetua stabilitas, veritatis vis, habere bonam causam, habet duos testes, vel tres, Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum.
units.tr: II. The second step of correction is given at Matt. 18.16: "But if he will not hear you, take with you one or two more" [Ἐὰν δὲ μὴ ἀκούσῃ, παρακάλεσε μετὰ σοῦ ἔτι ἕνα ἢ δύο], "so that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established" [ἵνα ἐπὶ στόματος δύο μαρτύρων ἢ τριῶν σταθῇ πᾶν ῥῆμα]. For after a private admonition has been rejected, the matter must not be brought at once before the Church. Instead we ought to take one or two others with us and press the admonition in their presence, because the admonition is confirmed by their testimony, either before the erring brother or before the Church which will later correct him. A single private admonition, and one given once in the presence of witnesses, is not enough. The brother who sins must be admonished, with patience and long-suffering, until he shows either repentance or obstinacy. If he hear you, if he does not hear you, if he refuses to hear them, Matt. 18.15, 16, 17. These words come from the law in Deut. 19.15, as the Septuagint translators render it. There the divine law wisely requires two or three witnesses in any case. It first rejects single testimonies, and then shows that a man's reputation can be such that not one witness alone, but two, establish the matter equally. For one witness is not enough in judgment. Hence among the Jews in the Old Testament no one was condemned on one witness; at least two or three were needed. So Jerome, in book 2 against Rufinus: "Not even Cato was believed on one witness." Num. 35.30: One witness shall not testify against any man that he die. Deut. 17.6, 7; 19.15; 30.19; Josh. 24.22; Ruth 4.9–11; Job 10.17; Ps. 27.12; 35.11; Isa. 10.12; 44.8, 9; Jer. 32.10, 12, 25; Dan. 13.40; Matt. 18.16; 26.60, 65; Mark 14.63; Luke 24.48; Acts 1.8; 2 Cor. 13.1; 1 Tim. 5.19; 6.12; Heb. 10.28. Jezebel too, wife of King Ahab of Israel, ordered two witnesses to be set against Naboth to accuse him, 1 Kings 21.10: you did curse God and the king. It is clear in itself that we are not teaching by these words that whenever two, three or more testify to something, it is at once true, and that the witnesses themselves cannot be counted false and lying. So there is no need here for allegory, which Augustine thought necessary to do when he treated this passage in Tractate 36 on John. He speaks thus: "In the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand. Truth is sought through two witnesses; human custom is plainly of this kind. Yet it can happen that two also lie. Susanna was pressed by two false witnesses. Are we to suppose that because there were two, they were not false witnesses? It is about two or three that the question is asked. The whole people lied against Christ. If therefore a people made up of a great multitude of men has been found to be false witnesses, how is it to be understood: in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand?" Unless perhaps this is the way the mystery of the Trinity is commended, in which there is perpetual stability and the force of truth: whoever has a good cause has two or three witnesses, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

units.tr: XXI.

units.la: III. Gradus correptionis v. 17. eipe ti ekklesia, dic Ecclesia, ubi per Ecclesiam intelligimus eos qui Ecclesiae gubernandae praesunt; his enim dicit, dic. Hoc est, notum fac, exponas, explanes, palam declares [Hebrew] coram Ecclesia; adhibuisti enim admonitiones privatas, & testibus adhibitis solenniter factas, quia admonitiones ex Scripturarum [Greek] contempsit, ignorans illud, aut studiose rejiciens. Ex praescripto legis cum docuerint te facito, Gen.42.18. Exod.20.23. Num.22.20. Deut.30.13. Josu.1.7. Jud.8.18. 1.Reg. 2.31. Psal.98.v.1. ne recedito ab ea sententia, dextrorsum vel sinistrorsum, Deut.17.11. & illud: vir ille qui commiserit superbe, ut non auscultaret sacerdoti, constanter ministranti, utique morietur vir ille, & tolles malum ex Israele, 12. affirmatio enim vultus illius, testatur contra ipsum, vae animo illius, quia affecit ille seipsum malo, Esa. 3.10. nec non illud quod Christus Dominus dicit, sit tibi [Greek] & [Greek] Ethnicus & Publicanus, h.e. profanus infidelis, Matth. 46.47. Peccator, Luc.6.32.33.34. & 15.v.1.2. alienus a fide Christi, qui vul- vulgò paganus & gentilis appellatur, 1.Cor. 5.1.& 10.20. 2. Cor. 11.26. 1. Pet. 2. 12. & 4. v. 3. cui sese hominibus adjungere nefas est, Rom. 16.17. 1. Cor. 5.11. Nunc autem scripsi vobis ne commiscea-mini, id est, si quis cum frater nominetur, sit scortator aut alieni avidus, aut idololatra, aut conviciator, aut ebriosus, aut rapax, cum ejusmodi ne edatis quidem, Tit. 3.10. Hæreticum hominem, post unam atque alteram admonitionem repelle, quia semel & iterum est monitus, adeoque jam constat de ipsius animo, ideo vers. 11. Scires quod talis eversus sit, h.e. prostratus jaceat, ⲯⲁⲧ vinctus à Diabolo, malâ voluntate, & concupiscentia, & peccet ita, ut sit à seipso damnatus, quia qui à conscientia victus, nihilo minus peccat, illius conscientia cauterio resecta est, 1. Tim. 4.2. qui quærit mortem; sed non invenit eam: Et cupit mori, & fugit mors ab eo, Apoc. 9. vers. 6. qui indignum judicat se æterna vita, Act. 13.46. qui dicit ligno, pater meus es, & lapidi, tu peperisti me, qui Deo obvertit cervicem, non autem faciem, Jerem. 2. v. 27. de quo dicere possumus, desperatum, quia dicit, decrevi, obstinavi, non accedam amplius ad te, Jerem. 2.31. qui ad Heb. 10.26. dicitur ultro peccare, hæc est ergo causa, quare dicat Apostolus repellere.
units.tr: III. The third step of correction is at Matt. 18.17: "Tell it to the church" [εἰπὲ τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ]. By the Church here we understand those who preside over the government of the Church, for it is to them that he says tell. That is, make it known, set it forth, declare it openly before the Church. For you have already used private admonitions, and admonitions made solemnly in the presence of witnesses, because he has despised these admonitions, which come from the Scriptures, either ignorantly or deliberately rejecting them. According to the law which they teach you, you shall do, Gen. 42.18; Exod. 20.23; Num. 22.20; Deut. 30.13; Josh. 1.7; Judg. 8.18; 1 Kings 2.31; Ps. 98.1. Do not turn aside from the sentence they pronounce, to the right hand or to the left, Deut. 17.11. And also: the man who acts presumptuously, not listening to the priest who stands ministering there, that man shall die, and you shall put away the evil from Israel, v. 12. For the look of their face witnesses against them; they proclaim their sin like Sodom, Isa. 3.9. Woe to their soul, for they have brought evil upon themselves, Isa. 3.10. Likewise what the Lord Christ says: let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector [σοι ἔστω ὥσπερ ὁ ἐθνικὸς καὶ ὁ τελώνης], that is, a profane unbeliever, Matt. 5.46, 47; a sinner, Luke 6.32–34; 15.1, 2; a stranger to the faith of Christ, who is commonly called a pagan and a Gentile, 1 Cor. 5.1; 10.20; 2 Cor. 11.26; 1 Pet. 2.12; 4.3. It is wrong to join oneself to such people, Rom. 16.17; 1 Cor. 5.11. But now I have written to you not to keep company with anyone who is named a brother, if he is a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such a one, do not even eat, Titus 3.10. Reject a heretical man after one or two admonitions. Because he has been admonished once and again, his mind is already plain, and so in v. 11: know that such a man is subverted, that is, lies overthrown and bound by the Devil, with an evil will and desire, and so sins that he is condemned by himself. For he who is overcome by his conscience and nonetheless sins, his conscience is seared with a hot iron, 1 Tim. 4.2. He seeks death, but does not find it; he desires to die, and death flees from him, Rev. 9.6. He judges himself unworthy of eternal life, Acts 13.46. He says to a tree, you are my father, and to a stone, you have brought me forth, and turns the neck to God, not the face, Jer. 2.27. Of such a one we may say he is desperate, because he says I have decided, I am resolved, I will no more come to you, Jer. 2.31. Of him it is said in Heb. 10.26 that he sins willfully. This is therefore the reason why the Apostle says to reject him.

units.tr: XXII.

units.la: Rejicimus ergò illam interpretationem, quâ Ecclesiæ nomine intelligunt, universam in Ecclesiâ multitudinem; His fulti argumentis. (1) Quòd Ecclesia Christiana in N.T. significet multitudinem, Presbyterium autem est collegium πρεσβυτερων, cujus collegii erat πρεσβυς, unum autem collegium non potest stare sine præside. Deinde (2) Quòd verba Christi, sit tibi tanquam Ethnicus, & Publicanus, non possunt referri ad tempora N.T. Sed ad Ecclesiam Judaicam. Prius ita diluitur ex 1.Cor. 6.v.1. Apostolus reprehendit Corinthios acriter, quòd cognitionem litium suarum non detulerunt sanctis; ubi non intelligit promiscuam multitudinem; sed illos qui in Ecclesia sunt, ut Ecclesiæ gubernationi vacarent, sicut Apostolus dicit sanctos quosdam ex sanctis, sic Christus dicit quosdam & præcipuos ex Ecclesia (1.) Quia secus sequeretur omnes fideles admitti ad recturam, cum tamen delinquentes ex illis velint excludi. Q.(2.) sequeretur omnes fideles monere non audientem, quia statim subjicitur, si Ecclesiam non audiverit; Quia (3.) Difficile dictu est, omnibus Ecclesiæ membris id indicandum ab eo qui offensus est: nam dicit, dic, tu nempe, qui offensus es; Etsi ergò agnoscamus cum totius Ecclesiæ clesiæ notitia hanc extremam disciplinam exercendam: ipse actus tamen tantùm à nonnullis abEcclesia deputatis debet exerceri, Act. 6.3. & 15.v.4.6. & 21.v.18. 1.Cor.5.v.4. & 12.v.28. 1.Tim.5.1. Act.2c.17. Phil. 1.v.1. Tit.1.5. Sic Tertullianus, Apologetico adversus Gentes cap. 39. describens conventus Ecclesiasticos Christianorum, Ibidem, inquit, etiam fiunt exhortationes, castigationes & censura divina: nam & judicatur magno cum pondere, ut apud cateros Dei conspectu, summúmque futuri judicii prejudicium est, si quis ita deliquerit, ut à communione orationis & conventus, & omnis sancti commercii relegetur. Præsident quoq; seniores probati, honorem illum non pretio, sed testimonio adepti; Ubi agit de gubernatoribus, quia dicit probati quique seniores. Sic Ambrosius in 1.Tim.5.1. in hæc verba, seniorem ne increpato &c. Apud omnes, inquit, gentes honorabilis est senectus, unde & Synagoga & postea Ecclesia seniores habuit, quorum sine consilio nihil agebatur in Ecclesia, quod qua negligentia obsoleverit nescio, nisi forte Doctorum desidia, aut magis superbia, dum sibi volunt aliquid videri. Quæ sententia patrocinatur constituendi in Ecclesia democratiam, quæ potius est ὀχλοκρατία. Alterum quàmvis sit speciosum futile tamen censemus. Nam solet Christus Dominus uti locutionibus ductis à consuetutine sui temporis, ad eas res significandas, quæ contingere debuerunt, post ejus ascensionem in cœlum, deinde & Paulus Apostolus N.T. temporibus usus est locutionibus ductis à consuetudine Ecclesiæ Judaicæ, 1. Cor. 16.22. nihil ergò gubernatores sibi præter rationem usurpent; sed jurisdictione à domino delatâ fungantur, ne quis ergò tale judicium ecclesiæ spernat, aut parvi æstimet se fidelium suffragiis damnatum, quia testatus est Dominus, istud ipsum nihil aliud esse, quàm sententiæ suæ promulgationem, ratúmque haberi in cœlis, quod illi egerunt in terra, habent enim verbum Dei, quo damnent perversos, habent verbum, quo resipiscentes recipiant in gratiam, Matth. 16.19. & 18. v.18. Joh.20.23. sine hoc disciplinæ vinculo, qui diu posse stare ecclesias confidunt, opinione sua falluntur, nisi forte carere impune possumus eo adminiculo, quod Dominus nobis necessarium providit: & sanè quanta sit ejus necessitas ex multiplici usu sagacius & melius perspicitur.
units.tr: We therefore reject that interpretation by which the name of the Church is taken to mean the whole multitude within the Church, for these reasons: (1) The Christian Church in the New Testament signifies a multitude, but the presbytery [πρεσβυτερων] is a college of elders, whose head was the elder [πρεσβυς], and one college cannot stand without a president. Next, (2) the words of Christ, "let him be to you as a heathen and a publican," cannot be referred to New Testament times but to the Jewish Church. The first point is refuted thus from 1 Cor. 6:1. The Apostle sharply rebukes the Corinthians because they did not bring the hearing of their lawsuits before the saints. He does not mean the mixed multitude there, but those who are in the Church, so that they might devote themselves to the government of the Church. As the Apostle calls certain saints "saints," so Christ speaks of certain chief persons in the Church. (1) Otherwise it would follow that all the faithful are admitted to the hearing of the case, although the offenders among them would want to be excluded. (2) It would follow that all the faithful must admonish the one who does not listen, since it is immediately added, "if he refuses to hear the Church." (3) It is hard to say that the one who has been offended must announce it to all the members of the Church; for he says, "tell it," meaning you, the one who has been offended. Although we acknowledge that this final discipline is to be exercised with the knowledge of the whole Church, the act itself ought to be performed only by certain persons appointed by the Church: Acts 6:3; 15:4, 6; 21:18; 1 Cor. 5:4; 12:28; 1 Tim. 5:1; Acts 20:17; Phil. 1:1; Tit. 1:5. So Tertullian, in his Apology against the Gentiles, ch. 39, describing the ecclesiastical assemblies of the Christians, says: "There also, indeed, exhortations, rebukes and divine censure take place; for judgment is given with great weight, as in the sight of God, and it is a very strong foretaste of the future judgment if anyone has so sinned that he is cut off from communion in prayer and assembly, and from all holy fellowship." Also "proved elders preside, having obtained that honour not by price but by testimony," where he speaks of the governors, since he says "proved elders." So Ambrose on 1 Tim. 5:1, in these words, "Do not rebuke an elder": "Among all nations, he says, old age is honourable; hence the Synagogue and afterwards the Church had elders, without whose counsel nothing was done in the Church. By what negligence this has fallen into disuse I do not know, unless perhaps through the idleness of teachers, or rather their pride, since they want to seem to be something." This opinion favours setting up a democracy in the Church, which is rather an ochlocracy [ὀχλοκρατία]. We judge the other view, though specious, to be nonetheless futile. For Christ the Lord is accustomed to use expressions drawn from the custom of his own time to signify those things which were to happen after his ascension into heaven; and Paul the Apostle, in New Testament times, used expressions drawn from the custom of the Jewish Church (1 Cor. 16:22). Therefore let the governors not usurp anything beyond reason, but let them exercise the jurisdiction committed to them by the Lord. Let no one then despise such a judgment of the Church, or think little of himself because he has been condemned by the votes of the faithful, since the Lord has testified that this very thing is nothing other than the proclamation of his own sentence, and that what they do on earth is held valid in heaven. For they have the Word of God by which they condemn the wicked, and they have the Word by which they receive back into grace those who repent (Matt. 16:19; 18:18; John 20:23). Those who trust that churches can stand for long without this bond of discipline are deceived in their opinion, unless perhaps we can lack with impunity that aid which the Lord has provided as necessary for us. And indeed how great its necessity is, is more clearly and keenly seen from its manifold use.

units.la: Hæc ego Censuræ verè, submitto piorum,
units.tr: These things I submit truly to the judgment of the godly,

units.la: Quos sparsos passim totus hic orbis habet,
units.tr: Whom this whole world holds scattered everywhere,

units.la: Ut, si errem, monear fraterna mente, fidéque;
units.tr: So that, if I err, I may be warned in a brotherly mind and faith;

units.la: Si non, ut mecum quisque probanda probet.
units.tr: And if not, that each may approve with me what is to be approved.

units.la: Nam non modò pium lectorem, sed & liberum correctorem, desidero. Atque sic candido lectori divinam benedictionem apprecatus; Zoilis vero, Momis, invidis, vel nihil, vel aliud agentibus, mentem meliorem, aut, si opus sit, helleborum. Benedic anima mea Jehova, & omnia intestina nomini sanctitatis ejus. Benedic anima Jehova, & ne oblivisceris ullius beneficiorum ejus, Psal. 103. v. 1. 2. Impleatur gloria ejus tota terra. Amen: iterum Amen, Psal. 72. v. 19.
units.tr: For I desire not only a godly reader but also a free corrector. And so, having invoked the divine blessing on the candid reader, but on the Zoiluses and Momuses, the envious, who do either nothing or something else, a better mind or, if need be, hellebore: "Bless the LORD, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name. Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits," Ps. 103:1-2. Let his glory fill the whole earth. Amen, and again Amen, Ps. 72:19.

units.la: FINIS. Veni Domine Jesu! TEKMHPION GRATI ANIMI,
units.tr: END. Come, Lord Jesus! A TOKEN OF A GRATEFUL MIND [TEKMHPION]

units.la: Quo
units.tr: Wherewith

units.la: Honori & Nomini Praestantissimi, Doctissimi Juvenis, Domini Stephani Gyöngyösi, Sympatriotæ sui charissimi, CLAVIUM potestatem orthodoxè propugnantis, litant: Nuper admirabili Dei providentiâ, & Principum Christianorum sympathetico auxilio, è jugo Triremium Hispanico-Neapolitanarum liberati, nunc autem Tiguri Helvetiorum, in molesto alioquin exilio, respirationem nacti, Ministri Ecclesiarum Hungaricarum infrà scribendi, 1676. Die 16. V. 26. N.S. Junii.
units.tr: They offer this to the honour and name of the most excellent and most learned young man, Mr. Stephen Gyöngyösi, his dearest fellow countryman, who vigorously defends the power of the Keys in the orthodox manner. Recently, by the wonderful providence of God and the sympathetic aid of Christian princes, he was freed from the yoke of the Spanish-Neapolitan galleys, and now, at Zurich in the land of the Swiss, in an otherwise troublesome exile, has obtained a breathing space. Written below by the ministers of the Hungarian churches, 16 May (26 June N.S.), 1676.

units.la: ARma sonant, lituíque crepant, bellona potentum Plebis & obscuræ corpora sternit humi:
units.tr: Arms clash and trumpets blare; the war-goddess of the mighty lays low the bodies of the common and obscure folk upon the ground.

units.la: At tu maganimo spernens fera prælia vultu, Armis pacificâ prælia mente geris:
units.tr: But you, with a magnanimous countenance scorning fierce battles, wage your battles with arms and a peaceful mind.

units.la: Insta vi, patriâ nomen virtute paratur: Quæ fecere patres, non ea nostra puto.
units.tr: Press on in strength; a name is won by virtue. What our fathers did, I do not think ours.

units.la: GEORGIUS KORMENDI, Hung. Olim E. Barsiensis V.D.M. nunc pro Jesu exul.
units.tr: GEORGE KORMENDI, Hungarian, formerly minister of the Word at Barsi, now an exile for Jesus.

units.la: MUndus ut immundus cum glauco mella veneno Offert, ut quæras, tu meliora solo.
units.tr: As the unclean world offers honey mixed with bluish poison, so you seek better things than the soil affords.

units.la: Huc ades, hic CLAVES, carmen, non paeonis artes, Invenies dulci mystica liba mero.
units.tr: Come hither; here you will find the KEYS, a song, not the arts of Paeon, and mystical cakes with sweet wine.

units.la: STEPHANUS KOMAROMI, Hung. Olim E. Refor. Jaurinensis V.D.M. nunc pro Christo exul.
units.tr: STEPHEN KOMAROMI, Hungarian, formerly minister of the Reformed at Győr, now an exile for Christ.

units.la: D
units.tr: D

units.la: VIS miser immundum peccator linquere mundum, Atque videre tui regna superna Dei? Dulcis Evangelii, dum vivis, crede ministris: Janua namque poli sic adaperta manet.
units.tr: Do you wretched sinner wish to leave this unclean world and to behold the heavenly kingdoms of God? While you live, believe the ministers of the sweet Gospel; for thus the gate of heaven remains open.

units.la: JOHANNES SZOMODI, Hung. Olim E. Szendiensis V.D.M. Nunc exul pro Jesu.
units.tr: JOHN SZOMODI, Hungarian, formerly minister at Szendi, now an exile for Jesus.

units.la: QUi bene de sacris disceptat CLAVIBUS, ille Quin bene, nil dubito, κλεῖδα[?] tenere sciat. In te quo Deus hoc verum doctissime quondam Esse velit, totus pectore, mente vovet:
units.tr: He who disputes well about the sacred Keys, I do not doubt, knows well how to hold the key [κλεῖδα]. In you, most learned man, whom God wills this truth to be, he vows with his whole heart and mind.

units.la: STEPHANUS BATORKESZI, Hung. Olim E. Orthodoxae Veszpremiensis V.D.M. nunc pro testimonio Jesu exul.
units.tr: STEPHEN BATORKESZI, Hungarian, formerly minister of the orthodox church at Veszprém, now an exile for the testimony of Jesus.

units.la: CLaviger esse velis coelestis, visque beatus Esse poli civis, Filius esse Dei. Hoc probat hoc fervens studium, quo praeceler ipsam Sic fidei normam mente nitente tenes.
units.tr: You wish to be a key-bearer of heaven, and blessed in strength, to be a citizen of heaven and a son of God. This eager zeal proves it, with which you hold fast the very rule of faith with a striving mind.

units.la: NICOLAUS LEPORINUS, Hung. Olim. E. Potariensis V.D.M. nunc pro testimonio Jesu exul.
units.tr: NICHOLAS LEPORINUS, Hungarian, formerly minister at Potary, now an exile for the testimony of Jesus.

units.la: DIsce Deum, tu dulce decus, morésque venustos, Ut ne coelesti destituare bono, Sacra paras clausi reserare palatia coeli? Coelestes animos, suscipe thura, preces.
units.tr: Learn of God, you sweet glory and graceful manners, lest you be cut off from the heavenly good. Do you prepare to unlock the sacred halls of the closed heaven? Receive, heavenly minds, incense and prayers.

units.la: PETRUS CSEGLEDI, Hung Olim Refor. Levaiensis, Eccles. V.D.M. nunc exul pro Jesu.
units.tr: PETER CSEGLEDI, Hungarian, formerly Reformed minister of the church at Léva, now an exile for Jesus.

units.la: TU sceptrum coeleste geris, telluris alumne: Errantes populos ad vada sancta voca. Luce Deus splendente tuos illuminet artus, Ut possis atavis non minor esse tuis.
units.tr: You bear the heavenly sceptre, nursling of the earth; call the wandering peoples to the holy shallows. May God illumine your limbs with shining light, so that you may be no less than your forefathers.

units.la: MICHAEL KARASZNAI, Hung. Olim. E. Kelemeriensis V.D.M. nunc pro Jesu exul.
units.tr: MICHAEL KARASZNAI, Hungarian, formerly minister at Kelemér, now an exile for Jesus.

units.la: C Unctos mortales cùm sit pugnare necesse, Assidui capito militis arma manu.
units.tr: Since anointed mortals must needs fight, take up the soldier's weapons with a diligent hand.

units.la: MICHAEL SZALOCSI, Hung. Olim E. Refor. Zubo- giensis V.D.M. nunc pro Jesu exul.
units.tr: MICHAEL SZALOCSI, Hungarian, formerly Reformed minister at Zuboly, now an exile for Jesus.

units.la: Firmus ut in studiis valeas, quæ recta teneto: Produc: néve sinas ut dogmata sacra tegantur, Claviger ut vigilans claudit, conclusáque solvit, Dispensat partes, cunctis sua præmia confert, Suspirans præco precibus sic clausa resolvit; Præstat pensa suis, cum fidus sacra resolvit, Corripit incautos, monstrans quæ sana sequantur.
units.tr: That you may be firm in your studies, hold fast to what is right. Bring them forth, and do not allow the sacred doctrines to be hidden. As the watchful key-bearer shuts and unlocks what is shut, so he distributes the portions and bestows rewards on all; the sighing herald with prayers loosens what is so closed. He gives their due to his own; when the faithful one unlocks the sacred things, he rebukes the careless, showing what sound things follow.

units.la: JOHANNES JABLONCZAI, Hung. Olim. E. Refor. Be- jeiensis V.D.M. nunc exul pro Jesu.
units.tr: JOHN JABLONCZAI, Hungarian, formerly Reformed minister at Bejec, now an exile for Jesus.

units.la: L Ætus ab excelsa missus sis nuncius arce: Hæc decorat teneram Regia virga manum.
units.tr: May you be sent as a messenger from the lofty citadel; the royal rod adorns this tender hand.

units.la: STEPHANUS ZEDENYI, Hung. Olim. E. Dörgicse- rensis, V.D.M. nunc exul pro Jesu.
units.tr: STEPHANUS ZEDENYI, Hungarian, formerly of the church at Dörgicse, V.D.M., now an exile for Jesus.

units.la: P Ande viam miseris, jussum ne sperne monentis: Sic volat immensum mens animosa polum.
units.tr: Show the way to the wretched, and do not scorn the command of the one who warns: so the spirited mind flies across the boundless sky.

units.la: MARTINUS SZ-PETERI, Hung. Olim. E. Hetenyiensis, V.D.M. nunc pro Jesu exul.
units.tr: MARTINUS SZ-PETERI, Hungarian, formerly of the church at Hetény, V.D.M., now an exile for Jesus.

units.la: U Nica salvandis ad cœlum janua Christus, Quam pandit CLAVIS: culpa remissa bonis. Unica damnatis, amissæ causa salutis, Quæ claudit cœlum, culpa retenta malis.
units.tr: Christ is the only gate to heaven for those who are to be saved, and the KEY opens it: sin is forgiven for the good. He is the only cause of lost salvation for the damned, and sin retained for the wicked is what shuts heaven.

units.la: THOMAS STELLER, Hung. Gymnasii Novi-Zoliensis olim Con-Rector, nunc pro Jesu exul.
units.tr: THOMAS STELLER, Hungarian, formerly co-rector of the gymnasium at Új-Zólyom, now an exile for Jesus.

units.la: P Ectora qui recreat pandens mysteria verbi, Ille aperit fidei cœlica regna Dei.
units.tr: He who refreshes hearts by unfolding the mysteries of the Word opens the heavenly kingdoms of God to faith.

units.la: NICOLAUS BUGANYI, Hung. Olim E. Gömörien-sis, V.D.M. nunc pro Jesu exul.
units.tr: NICOLAUS BUGANYI, Hungarian, formerly of the church at Gömör, V.D.M., now an exile for Jesus.

units.la: E Mentita ruit Papæ sub CLAVE potestas, Atque minax ejus fulmen, formidine mentes Mortales solvit, vilescunt mercis iniquæ Fragmina: dum Ductore Deo penetralia pandis Verbi sacrati; CLAVES ut jura capessant Proxima, sintque diu veris asserta Ministris. Rem magnam præstas; quis enim sua fulmina possit Extorquere Jovi? sed tu superare labores Heroum spectaris; ovans cum fulmina sæva Ab Jove Romano rapis, & victricia portas Arma, quibus victus, mundo non amplius optat Insultare, (: pudor si quis :) Regésque movere.
units.tr: The pretended power of the Pope collapses under the KEY, and its threatening thunderbolt, which held minds in mortal fear, is dissolved; the fragments of its unjust merchandise grow worthless, while, with God as your guide, you open the inner sanctuaries of the sacred Word, so that the KEYS may take up their nearest rights and be long maintained for the true ministers. You achieve a great thing, for who could wrest his thunderbolts from Jove? But you are seen to surpass the labours of heroes: exulting, you snatch the savage thunderbolts from the Roman Jove and bear the victorious arms by which, once conquered, the world (shame, if there is any shame) no longer wishes to insult or stir up kings.

units.la: VALENTINUS KOTSI, Hung. Scholæ Refor. Papensis olim Rector, nunc exul pro testimonio Jesu.
units.tr: VALENTINUS KOTSI, Hungarian, formerly rector of the Reformed school at Papa, now an exile for the testimony of Jesus.

units.la: Carmen gratulatorium ad Præstantissimum & Doctissimum Dominum Autorem & Respondentem, popularem suum, & peregrinationis Achatem.
units.tr: Congratulatory poem to the most distinguished and learned Lord, the author and respondent, his fellow countryman and companion on the journey.

units.la: JUlius arma parans Tyberina recondit in antra CLAVES, extollens talia verba, PETRI: Hic gladius Pauli nos nunc defendat ab hoste, Quandoquidem CLAVIS nil juvat ista Petri. Quid tu? bella petis? minimè; non Martis in aula Est pietas, bellis exulat ulla fides. Ergò quid? Ambabus CLAVES amplecteris ulnis Cœlorum, tentas queis referare polum. Euge tibi virtute pares, quod surgat ad astra Nomen, & obscuro ne capiare loco!
units.tr: Julius, preparing arms, hides the KEYS away in the caves of the Tiber, and utters these words about Peter: Let this sword of Paul now defend us from the enemy, since the KEY of Peter helps nothing. And what of you? Do you seek wars? By no means. Piety has no place in the hall of Mars, and no faith survives among wars. Why then? You embrace the KEYS of heaven with both arms, and you try with them to unlock the pole. Well done! You equal them in virtue. May your name rise to the stars, and may you not be caught in an obscure place!

units.la: JOHANNES KOTSI, Hungarus, S.S.Th. Str.
units.tr: JOHANNES KOTSI, Hungarian, S.S.Th. Str.
